MS-ADD-01879-00024.e: Fragment (leaves) 2 Leaf height: 205 mm, width: 137 mm.
MS-ADD-01879-00024.c: Bible ; This fragment consists of two folios from different parts of a Gospel book, copied in the 13th or 14th century. One folio contains part of the Gospel of Matthew, the other some short supplementary texts to accompany the Gospel of Mark, comprising two introductory hypotheses and two verse epigrams. Dr Christopher Wright

MS-ADD-01880-00001.e: Fragment (leaf) 1 Leaf height: 307 mm, width: 210 mm.
MS-ADD-01880-00001.c: Nicene Creed ; This fragment is a single folio from an Evangelion, containing one of the few known copies of Marcus Mamunas' Symbolon paraphrase . Little is known about this individual, who probably lived between the 15th and 16th centuries (PLP no. 16574). The text was found by I. Sakkelion in Cos in a 15th-century manuscript, now lost. The other witnesses to the text are two 16th-century manuscripts in Mount Athos ( Hagion Oros, Mone Iberon 535 (4655 Lambros) , Hagion Oros, Mone Megistes Lauras Ω 130 (1942 Eustratiades ) ). The text of the Symbolon or Creed, in 30 verses of 16 syllables, does not take into account the principles laid down by the Union of Churches of the Council of Ferrara-Florence (1438-45). The fragment was acquired by Constantin von Tischendorf and bought from his heirs by Cambridge University Library in 1876. Dr Matteo Di Franco

MS-ADD-01880-00002.e: Fragment (leaf)1 Leaf height: 291 mm, width: 183 mm.
MS-ADD-01880-00002.c: This fragment is a single folio, taken probably from an Oktoechos, containing the Stichera martyrika , a hymn sung during the morning office ( orthros ), in alternation with a psalm or scriptural verses ( stichoi ). The fragment was acquired by Constantin von Tischendorf and bought from his heirs by Cambridge University Library in 1876. Dr Matteo Di Franco

MS-ADD-01880-00004.e: Fragment (leaf) 1 Leaf height: 292 mm, width: 209 mm.
MS-ADD-01880-00004.c: Seven wise men of Greece ; This fragment consists of a single folio, probably extracted from the binding of a Latin manuscript codex. One side, now the verso, contains several Greek texts: two epigrams (the first attributed to Posidippus of Pella, the second Metrodorus' reply), the two Antistoicheiae by Maximus Planudes , followed by an extract from the sayings of the Seven Sages. The other side, now the recto, contains some psalms in Latin. The outer third has a slip of another leaf of the same manuscript, stuck on it upside down. The fragment was acquired by Constantin von Tischendorf and bought from his heirs by Cambridge University Library in 1876. Dr Matteo Di Franco

MS-ADD-01880-00006.e: Fragment (quire) 9 Leaf height: 219 mm, width: 154 mm.
MS-ADD-01880-00006.c: Greek language--Glossaries, vocabularies, etc. ; This fragment is a quire containing a brief extract from the Byzantine Lexicon of Pseudo-Zonaras , also known as Lexicon Tittmannianum according to the editor, J.A.H. Tittmann (1808). The actual authorship of this glossary is unknown, but it was traditionally ascribed to the 12th-century Byzantine historian John Zonaras. The arrangement of the glosses is alphabetical, by the first two letters, and later on according to grammatical gender and categories. The fragment bears masculine words only, and the beginning is repeated four times. The fragment was acquired by Constantin von Tischendorf and bought from his heirs by Cambridge University Library in 1876.

MS-ADD-01880-00007.e: Fragment (bifolium) 2 Leaf height: 219 mm, width: 156 mm.
MS-ADD-01880-00007.c: Libanius ; This fragment is a bifolium of a manuscript containing the Letters of Libanius , a Late Antique orator and teacher of rhetoric, probably copied during the 14th century. The bifolium was acquired by Constantin von Tischendorf (1815-1874) during travels in the East, from Sinai, Monastery of St. Catherine, Cod. gr. 1198 . This bifolium was originally between ff. 111v and 112r. Thirty-three more leaves from the same manuscript were donated by Tischendorf to the University Library of Leipzig, and today make up Leipzig, Universitätsbibliothek Leipzig, Cod. gr. 38 (Tischendorf 7) . Dr Matteo Di Franco

MS-ADD-01880-00008.e: Fragment (leaf) 1, Leaf height: 251 mm, width: 179 mm.
MS-ADD-01880-00008.c: Boethius, -524. De differentiis topicis ; This fragment is a single folio deriving from a codex datable to the 16th century. It contains some philosophical and rhetorical fragments, and the beginning of the Latin philosopher Boethius ' work De topiciis differentiis , translated into Greek by the thirteenth-century Byzantine scholar Manuel Holobolos. It was acquired by Constantin von Tischendorf and bought from his heirs by Cambridge University Library in 1876. Dr Erika Elia

MS-ADD-01880-00009.t: Possession note of a monastery on Mount Sinai
MS-ADD-01880-00009.e: Fragment (leaf) 1 leaf , Leaf height: 216 mm, width: 143 mm.
MS-ADD-01880-00009.c: Sinai, Mount (Egypt) ; This fragment is a single folio; it was probably originally an endleaf. It contains a Possession note of a lexicon from Mount Sinai , containing a threat against whoever would want to take the manuscript. Dr Erika Elia

MS-ADD-01880-00010.e: Fragment (leaves) 15 Leaf height: 167 mm, width: 250 mm.
MS-ADD-01880-00010.c: Hymns, Greek ; This fragment consists of two unstitched quires from a Theotokarion , a book of hymns to the Virgin Mary (the Theotokos), probably copied in the 14th century. The individual hymns - theotokia - are organised so that the first letters of each hymn form a series of acrostics, one of which survives here in its entirety, along with the latter part of the preceding acrostic and the early part of the following one. The first two sequences both contain errors, where the first letter of one hymn does not correspond to the letter which should appear at this point in the acrostic. The individual bifolia of these quires not being stitched together, there is an error in the foliation of the first quire, reversing the order of two bifolios. Dr Christopher Wright

MS-ADD-01880-00011.t: Refutation of the union of the Churches
MS-ADD-01880-00011.e: Fragment (leaf) 3 Leaf height: 201 mm, width: 146 mm.
MS-ADD-01880-00011.c: Schism Eastern and Western Church ; This fragment, taken from a 17th-century manuscript, contains an incomplete copy of the Refutation of the union of the Churches by patriarchs Philotheus of Alexandria, Dorotheus of Antioch, and Joachim of Jerusalem. The text comes from the Council of Jerusalem of 1443, in which the Eastern Patriarchs met to condemn the union of the Catholic and Orthodox churches, negotiated at the Council of Ferrara-Florence (1438-1439). The Patriarchs also condemned Metrophanes, Patriarch of Constantinople, who supported the union of the Churches. It was decreed that no clerk ordained by the Oriental bishops in communion with Rome should be admitted to exercise his office in their communion, until he had in the presence of the orthodox bishops proved his adhesion to the Greek Church. The Refutation is followed by some quotations from church fathers on the procession of the Holy Spirit in opposition to the Western doctrine of Filioque . In particular, the quotations attributed to Gregory of Nyssa and Cyril of Alexandria seem to have been taken from Gregory of Palamas, De processione Spiritus Sancti , whose order they follow. The fragment was acquired by Constanti

MS-ADD-01880-00012.e: Fragment (quire) 24 Leaf height: 202 mm, width: 148 mm.
MS-ADD-01880-00012.c: Propers (Liturgy) ; This fragment is made up of three quires containing the Akolouthia of St Kyriaki Martyr (7th July). An ἀκολουθία is the collection of hymnographic-poetic texts used by the church to celebrate a saint on his or her feast day in the service or office. The fragment was acquired by Constantin von Tischendorf and bought from his heirs by Cambridge University Library in 1876. Dr Matteo Di Franco

MS-ADD-01880-00013.e: Fragment (quire) 11, Leaf height: 200 mm, width: 145 mm.
MS-ADD-01880-00013.c: Dialogues, Greek ; This quire is part of a collection of fragments bought by Cambridge University Library from Constantin von Tischendorf's heirs in 1876. It contains a part of George Koressios's Dialogue with a Latin teacher ; the text is continued in Cambridge, University Library, MS Add. 1880.16 . Add. 1880.13 and 1880.16 were originally part of the same manuscript, together with another of Tischendorf's fragments, Cambridge, University Library, MS Add. 1880.17 . Georgios Koressios, native of Chios and renowned theologian, was lecturer in Greek at the University of Pisa from 1609-1615 and is known for his dispute with Galileo Galilei about floating bodies. Dr Erika Elia

MS-ADD-01880-00014.e: Fragment (quire) 4 Leaf height: 202 mm, width: 148 mm.
MS-ADD-01880-00014.c: Didactic poetry, Greek ; This fragment is a quire containing lines 78-229 of Michael Psellus' Poem on grammar , addressed to the emperor Constantine Monomachus. The verse are in decapentasyllabic and written continously as prose; the lines are separated by mid points. The fragment was acquired by Constantin von Tischendorf and bought from his heirs by Cambridge University Library in 1876. Dr Matteo Di Franco

MS-ADD-01880-00015.e: Fragment (quire) 6, Leaf height: 200 mm, width: 145 mm.
MS-ADD-01880-00015.c: Holy Spirit, History of doctrines ; This quire is part of a collection of fragments bought by Cambridge University Library from Constantin von Tischendorf's heirs in 1876. It contains a Fragment from a treatise on the Holy Spirit against the Latins . The text is written by an anonymous scribe, whose hand is also present in two other fragments in Tischendorf's collection, Cambridge, University Library, Add. 1880.13 and Cambridge, University Library, Add. 1880.16 , which, together with Cambridge, University Library, Add. 1880.17, derive from a single manuscript. MS-ADD-01880-00017.t: Three short texts in Greek about the Holy Spirit
MS-ADD-01880-00017.e: Fragment (leaf) 1, Leaf height: 195 mm, width: 145 mm.
MS-ADD-01880-00017.c: Dialogues, Greek ; This leaf is part of a collection of fragments bought by Cambridge University Library from Constantin von Tischendorf's heirs in 1876. It contains Three short texts in Greek about the Holy Spirit , written by two hands found in another of Tischendorf's fragments, Cambridge, University Library, MS Add. 1880.13 , therefore they probably derive from the same volume. MS Add. 1880.13, containing George Koressios's Dialogue with a Latin teacher , is from the same manuscript as Cambridge, University Library, MS Add. 1880.16 . A brown stain in the upper part of the recto of MS Add. 1880.17 near the edge matches a similar stain on f. 2 of Add. 1880.16, attesting that, at a certain point, these two fragments were located together. It seems likely, therefore, that fragments Add. 1880.13, 1880.16 and 1880.17 were originally part of the same volume. Dr Erika Elia

MS-ADD-01880-00018.e: Fragment (leaf) 1 Leaf height: 207 mm, width: 162 mm.
MS-ADD-01880-00018.c: Orthodox Eastern Church ; This fragment is a single leaf containing a page of the third Notitia Episcopatuum ( ed. Parthey 1866 ). The Notitiae Episcopatuum are the lists and hierarchical ranks of the metropolitan and suffragan bishoprics of an Eastern church, in this case that of Constantinople. This copy also presents the scholia and variants of the Codex Farnesianus , as they were printed by J. Freher in his edition of J. Leunclavius' Jus graeco-romanum (Frankfurt 1596) , tom. I p. 92. The fragment was acquired by Constantin von Tischendorf and bought from his heirs by Cambridge University Library in 1876. Dr Matteo Di Franco

MS-ADD-01880-00019.e: Fragment (leaf) 1 Leaf height: 137 mm, width: 101 mm.
MS-ADD-01880-00019.c: Prayer ; This fragment is a single leaf cointaining two Prayers in Greek , probably from a manuscript dating to the 17th century. The distinctive feature of the fragment is the drawing that occupies half of the recto. The fragment was acquired by Constantin von Tischendorf and bought from his heirs by Cambridge University Library in 1876. Dr Matteo Di Franco

MS-ADD-01880-00020.e: Fragment (quire) 9, Leaf height: 152 mm, width: 106 mm.
MS-ADD-01880-00020.c: This quire is part of a collection of fragments bought by Cambridge University Library from Constantin von Tischendorf's heirs in 1876. MS-ADD-01909.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedalakṣaṇa; Anukramaṇī ; The Ṛgvedasarvānukramaṇikāvivaraṇa by Jagannātha is a list of the various features (number of meters, attribution of meters to different deities, etc.) of the Vedic collection. It is "[a]lso called Anukramaṇikā-vivaraṇa or Sūkta-pratīka of Jagannātha. Although most catalogues enter and describe this as a commentary on the Ṛgveda-sarvānukramaṇī of Kātyāyana, probaby misled by the word vivaraṇa in the title, Haraprasada Sastri notes in his earlier Notices (L.) as well as in his later RASB catalogues that this is really a different text and an Anukramaṇī for the Bāṣkala-śākhā. Some of its Mss. are entered under different titles. Cf. also next entry Ṛgveda-sarvānukrama-prayoga." (Parameswara Aithal 1991: 233) The text contained in this manuscript is still unpublished. The manuscript consts of two codicological units, as the last leaf is a later supply.

MS-ADD-01910.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedalakṣaṇa; Vedavikṛti ; The Dīpikā is a commentray on the Jaṭāpaṭala —a text on the manner of recitation of the Vedic saṃhitā s—attributed to Hayagrīva. The commentary has been "composed in 1745 (Saṃ. 1801) at Vārāṇasī by Dayāśaṅkara, son of Dharaṇīdhara, surnamed Vyavahāra." (Abhyankar and Devasthali 1978: IV). The text is particularly significant for its thourough treatment of the topic of samaya (or galita ). The manuscript consists of two codicological units, as folios 4 and 5 are a later supply. It might prove particularly valuable for the history of the text, as it has been written only 33 years after its composition (Louis de La Vallée Poussin states that the commentary has been composed in 1821 Vikrama / 1764 CE; see LVP Add.1910).

MS-ADD-01911.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vaidika ; A paper manuscript of the Darśapūrṇamāsayājuṣahautra .

MS-ADD-01912.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vaidika ; A paper manuscript of the Darśapūrṇamāseṣṭi .

MS-ADD-01914.d: 1862 Vikrama / 1727 Śāka / 1805 CE (at the end of the Ṛgvedānukramaṇikā ).
MS-ADD-01914.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedalakṣaṇa; Anukramaṇī ; A multi-text manuscript containing Kātyāyana's Ṛgvedānukramaṇikā and Śaunaka's Anuvākānukramaṇī . The Ṛgvedānukramaṇikā of Kātyāyana is "a well-known general index to the Ṛgveda . It epitomises in the Sūtra style the contents of the metrical indexes"(Parameswara Aithal 1991: 216). The Anuvākānukramaṇī of Śaunaka is "a short index containing about 40 verses. It states the initial verse of each of the 85 Anuvāka-s of the Ṛgveda and the number of hymns contained in each Anuvāka. It also contains at the end some statistical details such as the total number of hymns (1017), verses (10,580 and half), words (153,826), syllables (432,000)."(Parameswara Aithal 1991: 90). The version in this manuscript is slightly different from the one found in Chandra Sharma's edition (1977: 43-47; for instance, the first 3 verses are missing).

MS-ADD-01915.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vaidika ; A paper manuscript of the Vaiśvānareṣṭi .

MS-ADD-01916.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vaidika ; A paper manuscript of the Aikāhikacāturmāsyeṣṭi .

MS-ADD-01917.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vaidika ; A paper manuscript of the Mṛgāreṣṭihautra .

MS-ADD-01918.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vaidika ; A paper manuscript of the Yājuṣapaśuhautra .

MS-ADD-01919.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vaidika ; A paper manuscript of the Śaṅkhāyanāraṇyaka .

MS-ADD-01920.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedalakṣaṇa; Anukramaṇī ; A multi-text manuscript containing two different texts. The first text in this manuscript is tentatively identified as the Ṛgvedānukramaṇikā (cf. Parameswara Aithal 1991: 239), possibly interspersed with an anonymous commentary that seems to start before the text (or by an unidentified independent text that precedes it). The second text is the Anuvākānukramanī by Śaunaka, "[a] short index containing about 40 verses. It states the initial words of each of the 85 Anuvāka-s of the Ṛg-veda and the number of hymns contained in each Anuvāka. It also contains at the end some statistical details such as the total number of hymns (1017), verses (10,580 and a half), words (153,826), syllables (432,000)" (Parameswara Aithal 1991: 90). The version in this manuscript is slightly different from the one found in Chandra Sharma's edition (1977: 43-47; for instance, the first 14 verses are missing). The manuscripts consists of two codicological units, as the first folio is a later supply.

MS-ADD-01921.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedalakṣaṇa ; The Svaritavākyapaddhati is an unpublished text on Sanskrit accentuation. It consists of a list of syllables of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā. This incomplete manuscript ends abruptly at adhyāya 20, verse 63.

MS-ADD-01922.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vaidika ; A paper manuscript of the Hiraṇyakeśīsmārtaprayogaratna .

MS-ADD-01923.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedalakṣaṇa; Śikṣā ; The Nāradīśikṣa is a well-known śikṣā ("Teaching [on Pronunciation]") belonging to the Sāmavedic school of recitation and included in the branch of knowledge known as vedalakṣaṇa . The text is divided in two prapāṭhaka s of eight kaṇikā each, and it contains a total of ca. 240 verses. It is the most important śikṣā as far as the connection between pitch modulations and musical notes is concerned. It is remarkable that a manuscript clearly produced in a Jain milieu contains a very technical treatise on pronunciation linked with Vedic recitation (see also manuscript Add.1924 , which most probably has been written by the same scribe, since it shares many common features with this manuscript: script, paper and layout are identical, and on the paper envelope used as original binding this manuscript is numbered as 2) 2, while Add.1924 is numbered 2) 3).

MS-ADD-01924.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedalakṣaṇa; Śikṣā ; The Gautamīśikṣa is a śikṣā ("Teaching [on Pronunciation]") belonging to the Sāmavedic school of recitation and included in the branch of knowledge known as vedalakṣaṇa . The text is divided in two prapāṭhaka . It provides a list of all the possible consonant clusters found in the Vedic text. The largest cluster mentioned contains seven consonants. It is remarkable that a manuscript clearly produced in a Jain milieu contains a very technical treatise on pronunciation linked with Vedic recitation (see also manuscript Add.1923 , which most probably has been written by the same scribe, since it shares many common features with this manuscript: script, paper and layout are identical, and on the paper envelope used as original binding this manuscript is numbered as 2) 3, while Add.1923 is numbered 2) 2).

MS-ADD-01925.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedalakṣaṇa; Śikṣā ; The Lomaśīśikṣā is a śikṣā ("Teaching [on Pronunciation]") belonging to the Sāmavedic school of recitation and included in the branch of knowledge known as vedalakṣaṇa . The Lomaśīśikṣā contains ca. 74 verses distributed in eight khaṇḍa s (“section”). As the great majority of the śikṣā s, it does not present a comprehensive account of vedalakṣaṇa knowledge, but focuses on specific phonetic and phonological observations as well as on aspects of Vedic recitation, in particular the musical notes. This manuscript has probably been written by the same scribe who wrote Add.1709 , another manuscript of the Lomaśīśikṣā dated to 1877, as well as Add.1710 and Add.1711 , and shares many common features with them (for instance, script, paper and layout are very similar, and they have all been bought in VārāṇasīProf. R. Griffith).

MS-ADD-01934.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedalakṣaṇa; Śikṣā ; The Maṇḍavīśikṣa is a śikṣā ("Teaching [on Pronunciation]") belonging to the White Yajurveda . It is included in the field of knowledge known as vedalakṣaṇa . It provides a list of words containing the speech-sound b.

MS-ADD-01935.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedalakṣaṇa; Śikṣā ; The Pārāśarīśikṣā is a śikṣā ("Teaching [on Pronunciation]") allegedly belonging to the pārāśara school of the White Yajurveda . It is included in the field of knowledge known as vedalakṣaṇa . Since it provides a list of the major śikṣā s belonging to the White Yajurveda , its actual composition is presumably quite late. The last stanza recorded in the present manuscript corrisponds to stanza 156 of the printed edition (1889-93; in 160 stanzas). This manuscript has probably been written by the same scribe of Add.1937 .

MS-ADD-01936.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedalakṣaṇa; Śikṣā ; An important śikṣā ("Teaching [on Pronunciation]") belonging to the Vājasaneyī school of the Yajurveda and traditionally attributed to Yājñavalkya. It is included in the field of knowledge known as vedalakṣaṇa . It shares numerous verses with other similar texts such as the Pāṇinīya and the Nāradīya śikṣā s, as well as ‏Uvaṭa's commentary on the Vājasaneyi-pratiśākhya . The text is known in various recensions. Regarding this manuscript, LVP notes: "Recension shorter than the printed edition (Benares Sk. Ser)".

MS-ADD-01937.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedalakṣaṇa; Śikṣā ; The Mādhyandinīyalaghuśikṣā is a śikṣā ("Teaching [on Pronunciation]") belonging to the mādhyandinīya school of the White Yajurveda . It is included in the field of knowledge known as vedalakṣaṇa . The text provides a list of substitutions of consonants (e.g. ṣ → kh, y → j) when these are found in particular clusters. This manuscript has probably been written by the same scribe of Add.1935 .

MS-ADD-01938.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedalakṣaṇa; Śikṣā ; The Lomaśīśikṣā is a śikṣā ("Teaching [on Pronunciation]") belonging to the Sāmavedic school of recitation and included in the branch of knowledge known as vedalakṣaṇa . The Lomaśīśikṣā contains ca. 74 verses distributed in eight khaṇḍa s (“section”). As the great majority of the śikṣā s, it does not present a comprehensive account of vedalakṣaṇa knowledge, but focuses on specific phonetic and phonological observations as well as on aspects of Vedic recitation, in particular the musical notes.

MS-ADD-01946.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedalakṣaṇa; Pariśiṣṭa ; A multi-text manuscript containing the Uktathaśāstra and the Kūrmalakṣaṇa , the twelfth and eighteenth pariśiṣṭa s of the Śuklayajurveda, by Kātyāyana. The Uktathaśāstra (also known as Uñchaśāstra ) discusses the Gṛhya rituals. The Kūrmalakṣaṇa discusses the Śrauta rituals (in 10 kārikā s).

MS-ADD-01947.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedalakṣaṇa; Pariśiṣṭa ; The Kratusaṃkhyā is the thirteenth pariśiṣṭa , attributed to Kātyāyana. It is a short text that discusses the Śrauta rituals.

MS-ADD-02079-00001.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedalakṣaṇa; Anukramaṇī ; The Anuvākapariśiṣṭa of the Vājasaneyisaṃhitā is "the fourth of the 18 Pariśiṣṭa-s of Kātyāyana. An index of the Ṛṣi-s, deities and metres of the verses of the Vājasaneyi-saṃhitā in the Mādhyandina school, including the Khila (Adhyāya-s 26-35) and the Śukriya portions (Adhyāyas 36-40)" (Parameswara Aithal 1991: 85). This manuscript is incomplete at the end, and most probably it has been written by the same scribe of Add.2079.2 , with which shares many common features (script, paper and layout are almost identical).

MS-ADD-02079-00002.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedalakṣaṇa; Śikṣā ; Fragments from the Yājñavalkyaśikṣā , an important śikṣā ("Teaching [on Pronunciation]") belonging to the Vājasaneyī school of the Yajurveda and traditionally attributed to Yājñavalkya. It is included in the field of knowledge known as vedalakṣaṇa . The text shares numerous verses with other similar works such as the Pāṇinīya and the Nāradīya śikṣā s, as well as ‏Uvaṭa's commentary on the Vājasaneyi-pratiśākhya . The text is known in various recensions. For instance, verses 20 and 21 of the present manuscript correspond to verses 55 and 56 of the edition by Tripāṭhī, and various other verses do not seem to have been included in the edition. Most probably, this manuscript has been written by the same scribe of Add.2079.1 , with which shares many common features (script, paper and layout are almost identical).

MS-ADD-02080.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedalakṣaṇa; Bhāṣya ; This manuscript contains the Vargadvayavṛtti by Viṣṇumitra, son of Devamitra, and the celebrated Ṛgvedaprātiśākhyabhāṣya by Uvaṭa. The first two leaves have been lost and the beginning corresponds now to Shastri 1931: p.3, II. 13-17.

MS-ADD-02087.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedalakṣaṇa; Anukramaṇī ; The Ṛgvedasarvānukramaṇikāparibhāṣa is the paribhāṣa portion of the Ṛgvedasarvānukramaṇikā of Kātyāyana. The text is "a well-known general index to the Ṛgveda. It epitomises in the Sūtra style the contents of the metrical indexes"(Parameswara Aithal 1991: 216). The independent transmission of the initial portion is a well attested phenomenon. The printed edition has only twelve kaṇḍa s, while this version of the text has fourteen.

MS-ADD-02092.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta; Jaina ; This 16th-century North Indian manuscript, probably from a Jaina scriptorium, contains Śaṅkara’s partly unpublished Aitareyopaniṣadbhāṣya . The version of the text transmitted in the manuscript, in nine books ( adhyāya ), differs substantially from the much shorter one, in three books, found in printed editions of Śaṅkara’s commentary since its first publication by Edward Röer in 1850. The Aitareyopaniṣad , belonging to the Ṛgveda , is generally held to correspond to books 4-6 of the second of the five sections (called āraṇyaka ) of the Aitareyāraṇyaka (see for instance Müller 1879: xcvii; Limaye and Vadekar 1958), and it is also often believed that Śaṅkara’s commentary covers only these three books (see for instance Potter 1981: 270-77, reprinted without change in 1998). The evidence provided by the manuscript suggests, however, that Śaṅkara commented on the whole of āraṇyaka s 2 and 3 (the latter also known under the title Saṃhitopaniṣad , found here in a final rubric). MS-ADD-02093.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of the Anubhūtiprakāśa by Vidyāraṇya. The Anubhūtiprakāśa , comprised of twenty adhyāya s, is a metrical treatise on Upaniṣads in line with Advaita Vedānta. Some manuscripts attribute this work to Sāyaṇa (NCC, vol. 29, p. 138). This manuscript is incomplete: it does not contain the first adhyāya .

MS-ADD-02094.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; An incomplete paper manuscript of the Bṛhadāraṇyakabhāṣyaṭīkā , a gloss ( ṭīkā ) on Ānandatīrtha's Dvaita Vedānta commentary ( bhāṣya ) on the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad. The gloss, also known as the Bhāvabodha , was composed by the 16th-century Mādhva theologian Raghūttama Muni, student of Raghuvatīrtha (also known as Raghuvarya Tīrtha). In this work, Raghūttama comments Ānandatīrtha's commentary, and often compares it with Śaṅkara's commentary on this Upaniṣad, criticising the latter (Sharma 1981: 465).

MS-ADD-02097.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of the Gauḍapādīyabhāṣyaṭīka , a gloss ( ṭīkā ) on Śaṅkara's commentary (known as the Gauḍapādīyabhāṣya or Āgamaśāstravivaraṇa ) on Gauḍapāda's Māṇḍukyakārikā s (also known as Gauḍapādakārikā s or Āgamaśāstra ). The gloss was composed by the well-known 13th-century Advaitin Ānandagiri, otherwise known as Ānandajñāna, disciple of Śuddhānanda.

MS-ADD-02098.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of the Kenopaniṣadvākyabhāṣyaṭippaṇa . This is a subcommentary on Śaṅkara's commentary ( bhāṣya ) on the well-known Kenopaniṣad . While a ṭīkā (or ṭippaṇa ) was written on Śaṅkara's commentary by Ānandagiri, the subcommentary here is different, though its author is not identified. The manuscript seems to contain only the commentary on the third khaṇḍa .

MS-ADD-02102.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Purāṇa; Śaiva Tantra ; This palm-leaf manuscript, probably of an early date (possibly 12th century), contains the Śivadharma corpus . The corpus, whose earlier texts possibly originated around the 6th century, usually contains from six to eight texts and deals with religious practices and doctrinal issues of the lay śaiva community. The present manuscript probably contained seven texts. However, as it is mutilated at both the beginning (the whole Śivadharmaśāstra is missing) and the end, it now contains only these six texts, and with several significant lacunas: Śivadharmottara Śivadharmasaṃgraha Umāmaheśvarasaṃvāda Śivopaniṣad Vṛṣasārasaṃgraha Dharmaputrikā

MS-ADD-02107.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of a commentary ( vivaraṇa , ṭīkā ) on the Sānatsujātīya . The commentary is traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara, and the manuscript concords with this tradition. The Sānatsujātīya refers to an episode of the Udyogaparvan in the Mahābhārata containing reflections on death, Brahman, and the virtues of brahmacarya . The episode in question contains five chapters ( adhyāya ); the manuscript contains only the first four chapters.

MS-ADD-02110.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Kāvya; Śāstra; Alaṅkāra ; A 19th-century manuscript, in the tripāṭha format, of Sarasvatītīrtha's Vidvadbālānurañjinī , an unpublished commentary on the celebrated Meghadūta by Kālidāsa. The author of the Vidvadbālānurañjinī "appears to be identical with the Āndhra scholiast Narahari Sarasvatītīrtha, who wrote a commentary on the Kumārasambhava , as well as one on the Kāvyaprakāśa entitled Bālacittānurañjinī . This last commentary gives us the information that he was born in Saṃvat 1298 (=ca. 1242 A.D.) in Tribhuvanagiri in the Andhra country. He traces his own genealogy from Rāmeśvara of Vatsagotra, and describes himself as the son of Mallinātha and Nāgammā and grandson of Narasiṃha, son of Rāmeśvara. When he became an ascetic, he took the name of Sarasvatītīrtha and composed his commentaries at Kāśī. He also refers to two works, Smṛtidarpaṇa and Tarkaratna (with its Dīpikā commentary), written by himself. The colophon describes Sarasvatītīrtha as Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakācārya. MS-ADD-02121.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vyākaraṇa; Cāndra; Bauddha ; This manuscript is the only known copy of the Dhātupārāyaṇa of Pūrṇacandra, a commentary on the Dhātupāṭha of the Cāndravyākaraṇa , listing the verbal roots of the Sanskrit language accompanied by concise meaning entries. As noted by Liebich (1902), who used this manuscript for his edition of the Cāndra Dhātupāṭha , in the extant portion of the work the treatment of the roots of each of the ten verbal classes ( gaṇa s) is confined to the present tense, called with the artificial term laṭ in the Cāndra and Pāṇinian terminology. The term appears in fact in the section rubrics of the manuscript. Liebich also remarks that the commentary shows traces of the influence of other Dhātupāṭha traditions (Pāṇini and Kātantra) despite Pūrṇacandra’s affiliation to the Cāndra school, which is shown e.g. by the form of the pratyāhārasūtra s found at the beginning of the work. The bundle also contains three additional folios, of seemingly related content, whose connection with the rest of the work is uncertain. The Dhātupārāyaṇa is as yet unpublished. MS-ADD-02124.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Nyāya; Navya-Nyāya; Vyākaraṇa ; A little-known tract on the meaning of Sanskrit compounds ( samāsa ) by Jayarāma Nyāyapañcānana, a 17th-century author belonging to the Bengali school of “New Logic” (Navya-Nyāya). Unlike his Padārthamālā , a manuscript of which is also kept in Cambridge ( Add.893 ), Jayarāma’s Samāsavāda is still unpublished, and manuscripts of it are quite rare. The work is probably identical with the one known as Samāsatattva (NCC 7.190), as can be easily inferred from its initial verse. Unfortunately, the second folio is missing and the text is interrupted on the last folio, in the middle of the explanation of copulative compounds ( dvandva ). The manuscript contains copious annotations, possibly by the main scribe.

MS-ADD-02137.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Manuscripts, Newari; Dharmaśāstra ; This Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript, written in Patan in 527 Nepāla Saṃvat (1407 CE) by a certain Rāmadatta, contains three works: a Newārī work on legal matters , a portion of a different unidentified Newārī text and the oldest recension of the Nāradasmṛti accompanied by a Newārī commentary-cum-translation (verse by verse or group of verse by group of verse), the Mānavanyāyaśāstraṭīkā by Māṇikya (or Maṇika), the author of the Abhinavarāghavānandanāṭaka , a drama preserved in Add. 1658.1 , as well as of a Newari commentary on the Amarakoṣa , preserved in Add.1698 (see also Shastri 1905: x and 43-44). The recension is the one normally found in Nepalese manuscripts as well as in the closely related text called Nāradīyamanusmṛti (see Lariviere 2003: 6). The text of the Nāradasmṛti starts with verse 5.8cd on folio 28r . The Nāradasmṛti is the only legal treatise from the first millennium that focuses solely on strictly juridical procedures, lacking therefore the portions on righteous conduct ( ācāra ) and atonements ( prāyaścitta ) common in other legal smṛti s. As already hinted at by Lariviere (2003: 1), it is highly possible

MS-ADD-02138.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Dharma ; A paper manuscript of the Rājadharmakaustubha .

MS-ADD-02140.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Kāmaśāstra ; A manuscript written in a Jain milieu, containing the Anaṅgaraṅga of Kalyāṇamalla, a 15th- or 16th-century erotic treatise composed for the Muslim aristocrat Lāḍakhāna, son of Ahmad of the Lodī dynasty.

MS-ADD-02141.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Kāma ; A paper manuscript of the Ratimañjarī .

MS-ADD-02142.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Darśana ; A paper manuscript of the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha .

MS-ADD-02143.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Nyāya ; A paper manuscript of the first section of the so-called Khaṇḍanoddhāraṭīkā by Pragalbhācārya (ca. 15th c., also known as Śubhaṃkara; see NCC, vol. 12, p.226). While the title suggests that this work is a commentary ( ṭīkā ) on the Khaṇḍanoddhāra - a work composed by Vācaspati Miśra II (mid 15th c.) to refute Śrīharṣa's Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya , an Advaita work refuting definitions of the Nyāya system (see NCC, vol.5, p.177) - it rather seems to be a direct commentary on Śrīharṣa's work. Firstly, Pragalbhācārya does not refer to Vācaspati's work either in his introductory verses or in the concluding passage of his work, but only to the well-known Naiyāyikas Śaṅkara Miśra and Vardhamāna Upādhyāya. Secondly, this work is also known as the Khaṇḍanadarpaṇa , and has been edited with other commentaries on the Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya in the Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series (1936).

MS-ADD-02144.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript including two works: 1. the Śaṅkaravijayaḍiṇḍima , a commentary on Mādhava-Vidyāraṇya's Śaṅkaravijaya (also known as the Saṃkṣepaśaṅkaravijaya ) by Dhanapatisūri; and 2. the Śaṅkaravijaya by Anantānandagiri (different from Ānandagiri, the 13th-century Advaita author of well-known subcommentaries on Śaṅkara's commentaries on Upaniṣads). The first work was written towards the end of the 18th century, and the second was possibly composed during the 16th century (Bader 2000). Mādhava-Vidyāraṇya's Śaṅkaravijaya and Anantānandagiri's Śaṅkaravijaya are two among many hagiographic accounts of Śaṅkara's life, the former being in all evidence the oldest available to us.

MS-ADD-02145.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Yoga ; A paper manuscript of the Haṭhasaṅketacandrikā .

MS-ADD-02146.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Śāstra; Yoga ; This manuscript contains a famous commentary on the Yogasūtra of Patañjali, the Rājamārtaṇḍa . The commentary is attributed to king Bhoja, who reigned in the 11th century, in Dhārā, central India. On the recto of the first folio , the text is referred to as the Bhojavṛtti , but the most well known title is possibly Rājamārtaṇḍa . However, Rājamārtaṇḍa is also the title of a text on jyotiṣa as well as a text on āyurveda (see MS Add. 2480 ), both also attributed to king Bhoja. The manuscript is incomplete, and the paper sleeve wrapping the manuscript notes that the manuscript contains only the commentary from book one to the 49th sūtra of book 3 (in fact, the numbering of the sūtra s in book 3 is erroneously advanced by one; the numbering jumps from 22 to 24, skipping 23, so that sūtra 49 in the manuscript should rather be numbered as 48; a second hand has corrected a few of these numerations in the margin). The Library holds another manuscript of this work ( Add.897 ).

MS-ADD-02147.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of the Yogavāsiṣṭhasāravivaraṇa , a commentary ( vivaraṇa ) on the Yogavāsiṣṭhasāra by Mahīdhara, son of Pūrṇabhadra and student of Ratneśvara (NCC, vol. 22, p.106). The Yogavāsiṣṭhasāra consists in a selection of verses taken from the Yogavāsiṣṭha and organised in ten topical sections ( prakaraṇa ).

MS-ADD-02148.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Nyāya ; A paper manuscript of the Anyathākhyātivicāra .

MS-ADD-02149.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Nyāya ; A paper manuscript of the Bādhabuddhivicāra .

MS-ADD-02150.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Nyāya ; A paper manuscript of the Māthurīdīdhiti .

MS-ADD-02151.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Nyāya ; A paper manuscript of the Tarkabhāṣābhāvārthadīpikā .

MS-ADD-02152.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Nyāyavaiśeṣika ; A paper manuscript of the Guṇakiraṇāvalīprakāśa .

MS-ADD-02153.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika; Navya-Nyāya ; One of the few extant manuscripts of Bhagīratha Ṭhakkura’s Dravyaprakāśikā (also called Dravyamegha or Dravyajaladā ), an unpublished commentary on Vardhamāna’s Prakāśa on the first section of Udayana’s Kiraṇāvalī . The author, sometimes nicknamed Megha (“The Cloud”), belonged to the Mithilā school of “New logic” (Navya-Nyāya) and was indeed, according to D.C. Bhattacharya (1958: 172), “a celebrated logician of Mithilā”. Probably born in Karijana (modern Kariyan, South of Darbhaṅga in Bihar) and active around 1500 or slightly later, he was the elder brother of the great Maithili logician Maheśa Ṭhakkura. Another brother of his, one Mahādeva Śarman, is mentioned in the second stanza of the present work (identical with the second stanza of his Nyāyakusumāñjaliprakāśikā ). It is believed that Bhagīratha studied under Jayadeva Miśra and was a contemporary of Raghunātha Śiromaṇi, who also commented on the section on quality ( guṇa ) of Vardhamāna’s Kiraṇāvalīprakāśa . Most of Bhagīratha’s works, some of which have been published (see Bhattacharya and Potter 2011: 196-207), are commentaries on treatises by Udayana or Vardhamāna, with

MS-ADD-02154.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Nyāya ; A paper manuscript of the Tarkasaṅgrahavyākhyānirukti .

MS-ADD-02155.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Nyāyavaiśeṣika ; A paper manuscript of the Ratnakośakārikāvicāra .

MS-ADD-02156.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Śāstra; Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika ; A 17th-century Jaina manuscript of Śivāditya’s Saptapadārthī . This short treatise, probably written around 1150 (Bhattacharya, D.C. 1958: 64), is among the earliest known works combining Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika. If the order of exposition of the text globally follows that of the Vaiśeṣika "categories" ( padārtha ), topics of epistemology are dealt with in some detail in the section on cognition ( jñāna ), one of the twenty-four qualities ( guṇa ). Śivāditya is also one of the first Vaiśeṣika authors to consider absence ( abhāva ) as a distinct category, a position originally typical of the Nyāya system. Several other works by Śivāditya are known to later Navya-Naiyāyikas (including Gaṅgeśa, who mentions Śivāditya by name), most of which have not been found yet. The present manuscript, dated 1682 saṃvat (= 1625-6 CE), is the oldest dated manuscript of a work on Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika kept in the Cambridge collection. According to the colophon, it was written in Campāvatī (possibly modern Chaksu, South of Jaipur in Rājasthān) for the personal study ( paṭhana ) of one Ṛṣiśrīsiṃhajī.

MS-ADD-02157.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Nyāya ; A paper manuscript of the Nyāyasārasaṅgraha .

MS-ADD-02158.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Nyāya ; A paper manuscript of the Tarkaprakāsikā .

MS-ADD-02159.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Nyāya ; A paper manuscript of the Tātparyavāda .

MS-ADD-02160.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Nyāya ; A paper manuscript of the Yogyatāvicāra .

MS-ADD-02161.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Nyāya ; A paper manuscript of the Īśvaravāda .

MS-ADD-02162.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Nyāya ; A paper manuscript of the Laukikaviṣayatāvicāra .

MS-ADD-02165.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of the Aparokṣānubhūtidīpikā , a commentary by Vidyāraṇya on the Aparokṣānubhūti (also known as Aparokṣānubhava , Aparokṣānubhavasudhārṇava or Aparokṣānubhavāmṛta ), a metrical treatise on Advaita Vedānta. Although the Aparokṣānubhūti is generally ascribed to Śaṅkara, it contains "views at variance with those of Śaṅkara, such as the denial of the Jīvanmukta being subject to Prārabdhakarman (verse 99ff.)" (NCC, Vol. 1, p.251). There are several editions of this work, with and without the commentary.

MS-ADD-02166.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of the Ātmapurāṇa by the 13th-century Advaitin Śaṅkarānanda Sarasvatī, the pupil of Ānandātman. Śaṅkarānanda Sarasvatī is also the author of a commentary on the Bhagavadgītā , the Tātparyabodhinī (see Ms Add 2169), and of several commentaries on Upaniṣads. The Ātmapurāṇa is a versified compendium on the principal Upaniṣads in eighteen chapters ( adhyāya ).

MS-ADD-02167.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of the Tattvadīpikā , a commentary by the 17th-century scholar Saccidānandayogin, student of Pūjyayogindra, on the Śrutisārasamuddharaṇa authored by Toṭakācārya. Saccidānandayogin is also the author of a gloss on Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Siddhāntabindu . Saccidānandayogin refers to the work upon which he comments as the Toṭakaśloka.

MS-ADD-02168.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of the Śukāṣṭakavyākhyāna by Gaṅgādharendra Sarasvatī, an Advaita scholar who flourished around the middle of the 19th century. This work is a commentary ( vyākhyāna ) on the Śukāṣṭaka , an Advaita poem in eight verses that celebrates the state of the individual who has achieved liberation while still alive ( jīvanmukta ), and that has been variously ascribed to Śukācārya, Śuka (Vyāsa's son), Vyāsa and Śaṅkara.

MS-ADD-02169.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of the Gītātātparyabodhinī , a commentary on the Bhagavadgītā by Śaṅkarānanda Sarasvatī, student of Ānandātman. Śaṅkarānanda was active before Vidyāraṇya (14th cent.) because the latter was his student (Dasgupta 1932: 57-58). The manuscript includes chapters ( adhyāya ) 1, 2, 7, 8 and the beginning of chapter 9.

MS-ADD-02170.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Nyāya ; A paper manuscript of the Jñānasvaprakāśatāvicāra .

MS-ADD-02172.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Nyāya ; A paper manuscript of the Praśnāvalī .

MS-ADD-02173.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of the third chapter ( pañcakośaviveka ) and fourth chapter ( dvaitaviveka ) of the Pañcadaśī by Vidyāraṇya, together with Rāmakṛṣṇa's commentary ( ṭīkā ). The Pañcadaśī is a well-known treatise of Advaita Vedānta, and has been published several times with various commentaries.

MS-ADD-02174.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of the Pañcadaśīviveka .

MS-ADD-02175.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of the Saṃjñāprakriyā , a short treatise listing technical terms of Vedānta with explanation. The author is not known.

MS-ADD-02176.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of the Siddhāntabindu by the 16th-century Advaitin Madhusūdana Sarasvatī. This well-known work of Advaita Vedānta is a commentary on the Daśaślokī traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara. It has been published several times with various commentaries.

MS-ADD-02177.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of the Āryavyākhyā by Saccidānanda Sarasvatī, who might be the same as Saccidānanda Yogīndra, the author of a commentary on the Śrutisārasamuddharaṇa (Adyar, vol.9, p. 357). His date of activity remains uncertain but he probably flourished during or after the second half of the 17th century: the Āryavyākhyā is a commentary on the Svātmanirūpaṇa (also referred to variously as Svātmaprakāśikā , Svatmānandaprakāśikā , Bodhāryā , Vedāntāryā , etc.), a work traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkara but more likely authored by Bodhendra Sarasvatī, who was a pontiff at the Kanchi Mutt towards the end of the 17th century. The Svātmanirūpaṇa is a short metrical work in the Āryā metre on Advaita Vedānta (Adyar, vol. 9, p. 354).

MS-ADD-02178.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A 19th century paper manuscript of Mahādeva Sarasvatī's Tattvānusandhāna . Mahādeva may have lived towards the end of the 17th century or the beginning of the 18th century, and is the author of another Advaita work, the Advaitacintākaustubha (Dasgupta 1932: 56), the Mīmāṃsānyāyasaṃgraha , a compendium of principles of Mīmāṃsā in the Bhāṭṭa tradition (Benson 2010), and the Sāṃkhyasūtravṛttisāra (see Benson 2010: 23, fn. 37). The Tattvānusandhāna , which includes four sections ( pariccheda ) was allegedly popular: it has at least three commentaries in Sanskrit and was translated early on in Tamil and Hindi (NCC, vol.8: 74-75).

MS-ADD-02179.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; An incomplete paper manuscript of the Tattvapradīpikā , an important treatise on Advaita Vedānta by the 13th-century Advaitin Citsukhamuni, student of Jñānottamamuni. See also Ms Add 2180.

MS-ADD-02180.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of the Mānasanayanaprasādinī (also known as Nayanaprasādinī ) by Pratyakṣasvarūpa (a.k.a. Pratyagrūpa), a commentary on the Tattvapradīpikā by Citsukha (13th c.), which is also included. Pratyakṣasvarūpa was probably active around 1400 (NCC, vol. 12, p. 276). The Tattvapradīpikā is an influential independent work in the Advaita Vedānta tradition, which has been edited a number of times with the Mānasanayanaprasādinī (see Bibliography). See also Ms Add 2179.

MS-ADD-02181.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of the Padayojanikā of Rāmatīrtha (early 17th c.), a commentary on Śaṅkara’s Upadeśasahasrī , also containing the mūla text. The manuscript includes only the first fourteen sections ( prakaraṇa ) and ends abruptly at the end of the commentary on verse 8 of section 14. There are significant variants at times between the manuscript and the Pândurang Jâwajî edition (1930); for instance, the second verse of the first prakaraṇa begins with idam in the manuscript, while the edition reads aham .

MS-ADD-02182.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of the Vairāgyataraṅga by a certain Sunātha, alias Bālapaṇḍita, the son of Śeṣapaṇḍita (Adyar 1951, pp. 368-369). This brief didactic poem of Advaitic leaning deals with the nature of renunciation ( vairāgya ).

MS-ADD-02183.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of the Vākyavṛttiprakāśikā by Viśveśvara Paṇḍita, an Advaita scholar of uncertain date who studied under Mādhavaprājña and authored commentaries on Advaita Vedānta works, including the Aṣṭavakragītā (see Ms Add 2441 and 2487), the Ātmabodha and the Dṛgdṛśyaviveka . The Vākyavṛttiprakāśikā is a commentary on the Vākyavṛtti , a short work in the form of a dialogue between a teacher and his student, traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkara and dealing with the interpretation of mahāvākya s.

MS-ADD-02184.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of the Vivekacūḍāmaṇi , traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara and very popular among Advaitins. The authorship of this work is disputed.

MS-ADD-02185.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vedānta ; A paper manuscript of the Mahāvākyaprabodha , which includes here two works: the relatively well-known Saṃnyāsagrahaṇapaddhati (which constitutes the largest portion of the manuscript) and the lesser known Nirvāṇayogapāṭhoccāraṇavyākhyā . The Saṃnyāsagrahaṇapaddhati , wrongly attributed to Śaṅkara, is known under various names: Saṃnyāsagrāhyapaddhati, Saptasūtrī/Saptasūtra, Saptasūtropaniṣad and sometimes Vedāntaviśrāntopaniṣad; it presents the gist of the ceremony of renunciation ( saṃnyāsa ) from an Advaita Vedānta standpoint. The transmitted texts of the Saṃnyāsagrahaṇapaddhati , of variable lengths and contents, would have been composed around the 16th century (Bouy 1994: 227).

MS-ADD-02190.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Bauddha ; A palm-leaf manuscript of the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā .

MS-ADD-02191-00001.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Bauddha ; A palm-leaf manuscript of the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā .

MS-ADD-02191-00002.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Bauddha; Tantra ; A palm-leaf manuscript of the Mahāmāyurīvidyādhāraṇī .

MS-ADD-02192.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vyākaraṇa; Cāndra; Bauddha ; A 15th-century manuscript of the Cāndravyākaraṇa of the Buddhist grammarian Candragomin (probably 5th c. CE) with its most widespread and best known commentary, the Cāndravyākaraṇavṛtti , for a long time believed to be the work of Candragomin himself, but now generally attributed to an author called Dharmadāsa who probably flourished in the 6th c. CE, but of whom nothing else is known (Dash 1986; Oberlies 1989). The manuscript contains the whole of chapter 1 and part of chapter 2. The text stops abruptly at the end of f. 113r , in the middle of the commentary on sūtra 2.3.37, gaurādibhyaḥ , as if the copyist was interrupted and never had the chance to complete the task. Folio 113v was left blank, although two verses, probably of a devotional or apotropaic nature, were later added by a different hand. This manuscript is among those used by Bruno Liebich for his 1902 edition of the sūtrapāṭha .

MS-ADD-02194.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Bauddha ; A paper manuscript of the Lalitavistara .

MS-ADD-02195.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Bauddha ; A paper manuscript of the Lalitavistara .

MS-ADD-02196-00001.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Bauddha; Bauddha Tantra; Dhāraṇī ; The Pañcarakṣā corpus ("Five Protections") consists of the Mahāpratisarā , Mahāmāyūrī , Mahāsāhasrapramardanī , Mahāmantrānusāriṇī , and Mahāśītavatī . The earliest evidence for texts grouped together as the "Five Great Dhāraṇīs" comes from Tibetan catalogues around 800 CE, but this compendium is somewhat different from the surviving Sanskrit collection, which is preserved in manuscripts dating back to the eleventh century. These scriptures include spells, enumerations of benefits and ritual instructions for use. With the course of time all of them became deified and five related goddesses emerged. It is, however, important to note that the texts themselves do not have any references to these goddesses. The kernel of this composite manuscript probably dates back to the 12th century. The many replament folios are from a much more recent date.

MS-ADD-02196-00002.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Bauddha ; A palm-leaf manuscript of a Dhāraṇi .

MS-ADD-02197.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Bauddha ; A palm-leaf manuscript of the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka .

MS-ADD-02198.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Bauddha; Bauddha Tantra; Dhāraṇī ; The Vasudhāradhāraṇī , dedicated to Vasudhārā, the bodhisattva of wealth, prosperity, and abundance (who has a strong following among the Newar Buddhists of the Kathmandu valley), is taught by the Buddha in Kauśāmbī to the rich merchant and layman Sucandra. He has been reduced to poverty and so requests a sermon from the Lord so that he may provide for his own family and so that all beings may become prosperous. This scripture includes a dhāraṇī along with enumerations of benefits and ritual instructions for use. This palm-leaf manuscript is probably to be dated to the 13-14th century CE. Its original wood cover are beautifully illuminated, although the illustartions are somewhat damaged.

MS-ADD-02199.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Bauddha ; A palm-leaf manuscript of an Unidentified Collection .

MS-ADD-02200.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Jaina ; A paper manuscript of the Antakṛtadaśāḥ, Anuttaraupapātikadaśāḥ .

MS-ADD-02201.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Jaina ; A paper manuscript of the Prajñapanā Bhagavatī .

MS-ADD-02202.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Jaina ; A paper manuscript of the Pratikramaṇavidhi .

MS-ADD-02203.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Jaina ; A paper manuscript of the Pākṣikasattarīsukhaprabodhinī .

MS-ADD-02204.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Jaina ; A paper manuscript of the Daśavaikālikasukhaprabodhinyavacūri .

MS-ADD-02205.c: Manuscripts, Prakrit; Śvetāmbara; Canonical; Chedasūtras ; A manuscript of the Kalpasūtra or Pajjosavaṇakappasutta dated V.S. 1578 (1521 CE), thus belonging to a fairly early phase. Its format, with narrow pages, is reminiscent of the format prevalent in palm-leaf manuscripts. The script of Kalpasūtra manuscripts is often calligraphic, of a squarish shape, like the one found in this copy. The simple colophon indicates that the manuscript was copied in Paḍihāra (unidentified location) by the Jain monk Matimeru for another monk called Vivekameru. The manuscript has marginal annotations which are probably by the hand of a later owner. A sentence in cursive script below the original colophon indicates that the manuscript seems to have changed hands, from a certain Haṃsājī to a Sahasā. The Kalpasūtra is a scripture belonging to the Śvetāmbara canon. It is written in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit. It is one of the most important works of the Śvetāmbara tradition since, especially in Gujarat, its public reading became associated with the festival of Paryushan, held in August-September, when everybody asks forgiveness for past errors. Mass production of Kalpasūtra paper manuscripts is evidenced fro

MS-ADD-02206.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Jaina ; A paper manuscript of the Paryuṣaṇākalpa with commentary .

MS-ADD-02207.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Jaina ; A paper manuscript of the Piṇḍaniryukti .

MS-ADD-02208.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Jaina ; A paper manuscript of the Saṃsthāra, Āturapratyākhyāṇa .

MS-ADD-02209.c: Manuscripts, Prakrit; Manuscripts, Gujarati; Jaina; Śvetāmbara; Chedasūtra ; This manuscript contains the Vyavahārasūtra , a Chedasūtra of the Śvetāmbara canon dealing with monastic atonements, in its original Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit together with a Gujarati quasi-literal translation. This is a type of commentary known as ṭabo because of its layout: the Gujarati part is above each line of the main text, written in smaller script, and is divided into small compartments where the Prakrit words are referred to only by their initial syllable. The manuscript lacks folios 15-17, hence part of chapter 4 is missing. The commentary has no title. The date is given as V.S. 1765, and seems to have been written by the hand who wrote the Gujarati translation. The Prakrit spelling is somewhat erratic. This type of manuscript is interesting as it shows how the reading of canonical texts was kept alive through translations in vernaculars which are close to reading notes.

MS-ADD-02214.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Jaina; Digambara ; This manuscript contains the first six chapters ( adhikāra ) of the rare work Dharmasaṅgraha of the Digambara author Medhāvin. Belonging to the genre of śrāvakācāra , the text deals with various topics of the right conduct of laymen, for instance with the five minor vows ( pañcāṇuvrata ) of a housholder. The text ends abruptly at adhikāra 7, verse 93. In its complete form the work consists of 10 chapters ( adhikāra s). The first three chapters set the context where the teaching took place: it is imparted by Mahāvīra, answering to the questions of king Śreṇika. This is the occasion for a detailed description of the Jina's samavasaraṇa . The detailed praśasti of the work has the following information: „The author of the Dharma-saṃgraha-śrāvakācāra tells us in his praśasti that Paṇḍita Mīha, a kṣullaka living at Hīsapura and a pupil of Jinacandra Muni, commenced this work during the reign of Firūz Khān of Nagpur and that he, Medhāvin, also a native of Hīsapura, completed it in saṃvat 1561 (!) , basing it on the writings of Samantabhadra, Vasunandin, and Āśādhara.“ (Williams 1963: 30 and Śāstrī 1979: 224-231). MS-ADD-02220.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Jaina; Śvetāmbara; Narrative literature relating to early Jain teachers ; A manuscript of Samayasundara's Kālakācāryakathā . Samayasundara's version of this story, one among numerous renderings in Prakrit, Sanskrit or Gujarati, was composed in 1609 (V.S. 1666) in Bikaner. The author is a Śvetāmbara Jain monk from the Kharataragaccha, and a prolific and learned author of several compositions in Sanskrit, Prakrit and Gujarati. This text is both in verse and in prose and makes use of all three languages. It belongs to the 'later encyclopedic versions' of the story, 'that draws from all foregoing versions and possibly also from oral sources. The expansion of the Gardabhilla episode is especially marked' (Norman Brown 1933: 34). The Kālakācāryakathā , the story of the Jain monk Kālaka, is one of the most famous legends and one of the most often illustrated Jain Śvetāmbara works. It is often appended to the Kalpasūtra , because both have a strong connection with the eight-day Jain festival of Paryushan (August /September) which marks the climax of the rainy season. MS-ADD-02221-00004.c: Manuscripts, Gujarati; Jaina; Śvetāmbara, narrative ; This part of the manuscript contains the 2nd and 3rd chapter ( khaṇḍa ) of the Añjanasundarīcaupaī , a Śvetāmbara narrative text in Gujarati language. The author Puṇyasāgara was a pupil of Karmasāgarasūri of the Pīṃpalagaccha. Composed in V.S. 1689, the work deals with the story of Añjanasundarī's marriage with prince Pavanañjaya, son of king Prahlāda (for details see Balbir 2006: Cat. No. 825). The scribe Gajavijaya was a pupil of Tejavijayamuni, who was a pupil of Vijayasiṃhasūri under the pontiff Vijayadevasūri of the Tapāgaccha. This lineage is also given at the end of the work Śrīpālacaritrarāsa by Jinavijaya (see Schubring 1944: Cat. No. 1093).

MS-ADD-02223.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Manuscripts, Prakrit; Jaina; Śvetāmbara; Cosmology ; This is a manuscript of the Laghukṣetrasamāsavṛtti , a commentary written in Sanskrit by Haribhadrasūri. According to the commentator's colophon itself the date of composition is V.S. 1185 = 1128 CE. The text commented upon consists of 109 verses in Jaina Māhārāṣṭrī Prakrit which are found in the Samayakhettasamāsa or Kṣetrasamāsa written by Jinabhadra between V.S. 545 and V.S. 650 (Leumann 1934: 55a and 55b: 'eine 109-strophige Recension ist von Haribhadra commentirt worden'; Leumann No. 204 in Plutat 1998; Desai 1968: 168-169). Haribhadra's commentary is chronologically the first. Other commentaries of this work in longer recensions exist. The largest one is that of Malayagiri (V.S. 1200). The Cambridge manuscript is valuable as not so many manuscripts of this text with Haribhadra's commentary seem to be available even in India, a fortiori outside India (see bibliography). In addition the Cambridge manuscript is dated and old: it was copied in V.S. 1491 = 1434 CE in Ajmer, Rajasthan. The copyist is Kamalacandragaṇi, pupil of Jayaśekhara, from the Kṛṣṇarṣigaccha. MS-ADD-02232.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Jaina; Śvetāmbara, narrative ; This anonymous Samyakvakaumudī is a collection of eight tales ( kathānaka ) „in which the merchant Arhaddāsa tells his eight wifes, and they in turn tell him, how they attained to perfection (samyaktva) in religion. MS-ADD-02248.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Śaiva; Tantra; Karmakāṇḍa ; This palm-leaf manuscript written in Nepālākṣarā contains the complete Jñānadīpavimarśiṇī of Vidyānandanātha, also known as the Tripurasundarīpaddhati (even though there appears to be also a different work under this name: see for instance manuscripts under this name in the NGMCP catalogue, and a note to this effect by La Vallée Poussin, LVP Add.2248). The manuscript probably dates to the fourteenth or fifteenth century CE. The Jñānadīpavimarśiṇī is a ritual manual covering rites related to the worship of the godess Triprasundarī of the Śrīvidyā tradition. The author Vidyānandanātha was active in South India during the thirteenth century (Sanderson forthcoming), and is probably also the author of the Artharatnāvalī , a commentary on the Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava .

MS-ADD-02249.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Dhanurveda; Śaiva ; This palm-leaf manuscript contains an unidentified work of dhanurveda (the knowledge of archery and weaponry), consisting of a dialogue between Śiva and Pārvati. According to a note in Bendall's Journey to Nepal , page 59, it is "by far the smallest palm leaf MS yet found in Nepal".

MS-ADD-02251-00001.d: Possibly 13th century CE. Note: As the final folios with the colophon are missing, the manuscript is undated, but it looks very old. Although exact parallels are hard to find, its script resembles that of a manuscript of the Mohacūḍottara kept in the National Archives of Kathmandu, Nepal (Acc. NAK 4/1622 = NGMCP B 27/18), dated 806, which according to Diwakar Acharya is a date of the Valabhi era, therefore corresponding to 1125 CE (see Tāntrikābhidhānakośa II , p. 174, s.v. gaṇa ). This suggests a western or central Indian origin also for the Cambridge manuscript. It is worth noting that Yaśodhara, the author of the Jayamaṅgala , is generally assigned to the 13th century. If the latter date is reliable, Add.2251.1 would be an early copy of Yaśodhara’s work prepared not long after its composition, possibly from a source in a different script that the scribe did not know well, since complex ligatures (i.e. consonant clusters) are often erroneously reproduced.
MS-ADD-02251-00001.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Kāmaśāstra ; The Jayamaṅgalā of Yaśodhara (possibly, fl. 13th century), the most important commentary on the famous Kāmasūtra of Vātsyāyana Mallanāga. The manuscript contains an almost complete text of the commentary, but not the mūla text. Despite being nicely written, the text is quite corrupt and has frequent lacunae, indicated by dashes above the line. The bundle also includes one folio of another copy of the same text (see Add.2251.2 ), probably by the same hand, and a one-leaf fragment of Kālidāsa's Kumārasambhava in Nepalākṣara script (see Add.2251.3 ).

MS-ADD-02251-00002.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Kāmaśāstra ; This leaf, bearing the folio number 80, is a fragment of the Jayamaṅgalā of Yaśodhara (possibly, fl. 13th century), a commentary on the Kāmasūtra of Vātsyāyana Mallanāga. At some point in the history of manuscript Add.2151.1 , containing the same text, this folio was inserted by mistake in place of the original f. 80. The latter is still preserved in the same bundle as an extra folio at the end (together with another fragment, Add.2151.3). Interestingly, Add.2151.1 and Add.2251.2 are clearly written by the same hand and are on the same kind of palm leaf, which explains how the exchange might have taken place. Despite bearing the folio number 80, it roughly corresponds to f. 50 of Add.2151.1 , namely a much earlier section of the text (Jayamaṅgalā ad Kāmasūtra 1.5.7-12). This suggests that the copyist may have made two copies of the same text, possibly around the same time, one ( Add.2151.1 ) with the commentary alone and the other, to which this folio belonged, in which the commentary was preceded by the main text. This might explain the discrepancy in folio numbers between the two folios containing the same section.

MS-ADD-02251-00003.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Kāvya ; This single leaf contains the first 15 verses of sarga 5 of Kālidāsa's Kumārasambhava . It breaks off in the middle of verse 15. It is found in the same bundle as Add.2251.1 and 2251.2 ( Jayamaṅgalā ), to which it is not related in any way, although it appears to be equally old. Both the kind of palm leaf and the script are in fact entirely different. It is not known when this leaf was added to the bundle nor by whom.

MS-ADD-02252.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Manuscripts, Prakrit; Jaina; Śvetāmbara, canonical. ; This manuscript contains Abhayadeva's Sanskrit commentary on the eighth Aṅga of the Śvetāmbara canon, a narrative text in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit, telling stories of various characters who “put an end” ( anta-kr̥t ) to rebirths. Many of them belong to the time of the twenty-second Jina, Ariṣṭanemi, and some of them relate to the Kr̥ṣṇa cycle. This manuscript is especially valuable because it belongs to a set of the 45 Śvetāmbara āgama s commissioned by the members of the same family. The set is now scattered among different libraries. Some items have been traced in Berlin and in India (see Balbir 2006, pp. 325-52). The colophon is identical in all items traced. It always indicates the place of the copied manuscript within the group by a phrase of the type “manuscripts of the 45 Āgamas have been made to copy. Among them this is the 10th Aṅga/Upāṅga, etc.” The name of the donor is given as Jayakaraṇa, a resident of Khambhat. He and his family members systematically collected manuscripts of the Śvetāmbara canonical texts (See Balbir 2006 and Balbir 2013). The Cambridge University Library has two items belonging

MS-ADD-02255.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Manuscripts, Prakrit; Jaina; Śvetāmbara, Aṅga ; This is a manuscript of Abhayadeva's Sanskrit commentary on the eleventh Aṅga of the Śvetāmbara canon, the Vipākasūtra , a narrative work about the consequences of bad behaviours in the first part ( śrutaskandha) called Duḥkhavipāka and those of good behaviours in the second part called Sukhavipāka . The first part, the longest, is divided into ten chapters which are distributed as follows here: chap. 1 ends on f. 5v4 ; 2 on f. 9v7 ; 3 on f. 13r4 ; 4 on f. 13r15 ; 5 on f. 13v3 ; 6 on f. 14v5 ; 7 on f. 16r1 ; 8 on f. 16v5 ; 9 on f. 17v7 ; 10 on f. 17v9 . The remaining part is occupied by the second part, which is much shorter as only the first story is told fully. The others are repetitions of the main pattern. Abhayadevasūri is one of the most famous Jain commentators. He lived in the 11th century and is known as navāṅgīvṛttikāra since he wrote a commentary on nine of the eleven Aṅgas of the Śvetāmbara canon. This manuscript has two folios numbered 1. The first one is from one hand, the second folio numbered as 1 is from another hand by which all the rest was copied. There is no gap in the text as the last sente

MS-ADD-02256.c: Manuscripts, Prakrit; Jaina; Śvetāmbara, canonical. ; This manuscript contains five texts that are usually found together: Nirayāvalikā , Kalpāvataṃsikā , Puṣpikā , Puṣpacūlā and Vṛṣṇidaśā . They correspond to the last five Upāṅgas of the Śvetāmbara canon. According to the colophon, the manuscript was commissioned by Budhakheṭāka, son of Buharāḍhāla, in order to be read by Devavijayagaṇi, during the reign of the famous Hīravijayasūri, pontiff of the Tapāgaccha .

MS-ADD-02257.c: Manuscripts, Prakrit; Jaina; Śvetāmbara, canonical ; The Sthānāṅgasūtra , or Ṭhānāṅgasutta in its Prakrit form, is the 3rd Aṅga of the Śvetāmbara canon. It is an encyclopaedic work divided into ten chapters ( sthāna ) consisting of lists relating to doctrine, practice, mythology, cosmogology etc. This 16th century manuscript was written for the study of Kābā, pupil of Vijayadānasūri of the Tapāgaccha.

MS-ADD-02266.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Kāvya ; The Kumārasambhava by Kālidāsa has been called "the greatest long poem in classical Sanskrit, by the greatest poet of the language" (Heifetz 1985: 1). Some manuscripts contain up to seventeen sarga s, but only the first eight are commonly ascribed to be the work of Kālidāsa himself. This manuscript contains the first seven sarga s of the text. The eighth sarga , a vivid description of the 25-year long lovemaking between Śiva and Pārvatī, was sometimes omitted by medieval scribes due to its erotic content. Editions omitting the eighth sarga have also been published, some of which are intended for use in schools (Heifetz 1985: 6). This manuscript, probably written in a Jain scriptorium, contains copious marginal annotations. The scribe, Lāvaṇyavimala, is named in the colophon, as well as his teacher, Śrīdānavimala.

MS-ADD-02268.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Manuscripts, Prakrit; Jaina; Śvetāmbara, canonical ; Traditionally attributed to Bhadrabāhu the Kalpasūtra is a major canonical text of the Śvetāmbara Jains, composed in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit, in a mixture of prose and verse, and containing the life-stories of the twenty-four Jinas, in particular Neminātha, Pārśvanātha and Mahāvīra. This Avacūri was composed by Kulamaṇḍanasūri on the basis of Jinaprabhasūri's commentary Sandehaviṣauṣadhi, 14th century. It is also called Antarvācanā , „a sort of indirect commentary. It narrates the legends suggested in the text and explains the ritual connected with the reading of the Kalpasūtra “ (Velankar 1944: p. 78). Kulamaṇḍanasūri was one of the five prominent disciples of Devasundarasūri, the 49th pontiff of the Tapāgaccha. He was born in V.S. 1409, became Sūri in V.S. 1442 and died in V.S. 1455 (cf. Klatt 1882: p. 255). Based on these dates, this Avacūri can be dated between V.S. 1442 and V.S. 1455. He composed also an Avacūri on the Prajñāpanātṛtīyapadasaṁgrahaṇī (cf. Balbir 2006: Cat. No. 80).

MS-ADD-02277.c: Manuscripts, Prakrit; Jaina; Śvetāmbara; Ethics, general teaching ; This manuscript contains the last eight chapters of the Yogaśāstra , composed by the 12th century Jain monk and teacher Hemacandra. This comprehensive treatise on Śvetāmbara Jainism consists of 12 chapters which were usually handed down in two parts, namely chapters 1-4 and 5-12. Jaina manuscript collections include mostly more manuscripts which contain the first four chapters since they deal with important topics of the Jaina doctrine. The last eight chapters mainly concern themes of breath control, meditation and divination.

MS-ADD-02280.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Manuscripts, Prakrit; Jaina; Śvetāmbara, canonical ; This manuscript contains an anonymous Sanskrit commentary ( avacūri ) on the Daśavaikālikasūtra , the 2nd Mūlasūtra of the Śvetāmbara canon. The Sūtra is ascribed to the monk Śayambhava (or Sijjaṃbhava in its Prakrit form) who is mentioned in verse 17 and 20 on folio 20v . The last four stanzas are originally taken from the Daśavaikālikaniryukti. This concise treatise deals with the correct ascetic behaviour; it consists of ten chapters ( ajjhayaṇa ) and the two cūlikā s. A manuscript which contains the same avacūri is described in Weber Cat. No. 1921.

MS-ADD-02286.c: Manuscripts, Prakrit; Jaina; Śvetāmbara, canonical ; The Jñātādharmakathā is the sixth Aṅga of the Śvetāmbara canon, a narrative text in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit with short parables and extensive legends. The most famous are section 8 about Mallī, the 19th Jina who, according to the Śvetāmbaras, was a woman, and section 16, which is a Jain version of the Mahābhārata . This manuscript is especially valuable because it belongs to a set of the 45 Śvetāmbara āgama s commissioned by the members of the same family. This set is now scattered among different libraries. Some items have been traced in Berlin and in India (see Balbir 2006: 325-352). The colophon is identical in all items traced. It always indicates the place of the copied manuscript within the group by a phrase of the type "manuscripts of the 45 Āgamas have been made to copy. Among them this is the 10th Anga/Upāṅga, etc." In this case, the colophon also gives the name of the donor, Jayakaraṇa, a resident of Khambhat; he and his family members systematically collected manuscripts of the Śvetāmbara canonical works (see Balbir 2006 and Balbir 2013). MS-ADD-02304.c: Manuscripts, Prakrit; Jaina; Śvetāmbara; Cosmology ; This is a manuscript of the Narakhittaviyāra "Reflection about the area of humans" [in the Jain universe] by Somatilakasūri, also known as Navyakṣetrasamāsa or Bṛhatkṣetrasamāsa . It is written in Jaina Māhārāṣṭrī Prakrit and has 388 verses: verse 100 is on f.3r ; verse 200 is on f.5r , line 7; verse 300 is on f.7r , line 9. This cosmological work was composed around 1340 CE and belongs to the intermediate phase of Jain cosmological writings (compared to the earlier one represented by Jinabhadragaṇi, 6th century, and the later one represented by Vinayavijaya in the 17th century). Somatilakasūri belonged to the Tapāgaccha. This is a very significant manuscript because of its old age and because outside India manuscripts having the Prakrit text of Somatilakasūri without commentary are relatively rare, as is shown by Velankar (1944). MS-ADD-02313.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Jaina; Vyākaraṇa ; The Śabdānuśāsana , or Siddhahaimacandra , by the 12th century Jain polymath Hemacandra consists of 8 chapters ( adhyāya ) of four sections ( pāda ) each, dealing with Sanskrit grammar in the first seven chapters and with Prakrit grammar in the eighth chapter. He composed two commentaries on his work, a long version ( bṛhadvṛtti ) and a short version ( laghuvṛtti ). This 15th century manuscript contains chapter I-III.2 of the Śabdānuśāsanalaghuvṛtti dealing with the sandhi, noun, case and compounds (cf. Balbir 2006, vol. 3: p. 451). This manuscript was commissioned by Cāritradharma, a pupil of Lakṣmīsāgarasūri. From a later hand on folio 22v we learn that this manuscript was deposited in the library of Raṅgavijaya, disciple of Harṣavijayagaṇi.

MS-ADD-02314.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Jaina; Vyākaraṇa ; The Śabdānuśāsana , or Siddhahaimacandra , by the 12th century Jain polymath Hemacandra consists of 8 chapters ( adhyāya ) of four sections ( pāda ) each, dealing with Sanskrit grammar in the first seven chapters and with Prakrit grammar in the eighth chapter. He composed two commentaries on his work, a long version ( bṛhadvṛtti ) and a short version ( laghuvṛtti ). This 15th century manuscript contains chapter one and two (up to the second pāda ) of the Śabdānuśāsanalaghuvṛtti dealing with technical terms ( saṃjñā ), vowels ( svara ), consonants ( vyañjana ), nouns ( nāman ) and cases ( kāraka ). The 8th chapter ( adhyāya ) is divided in four sections ( pāda ) dealing with phonetics, adverb, noun, verb and Prakrit dialects like Śaurasenī, Māghadhī, Paiśācī, Cūlikāpaiśācikā and Apabhraṃśa. The four stanzas after the final rubric beginning with āsīd viśāṃ patir on folio 32r6 are printed in Pischel 1877: p. V. At the end is a praśasti in eleven stanzas given. It informs us about the layman Aulāsiṃha of the Prāgvaṭa family. From his wife, Meghādevī, he had one son Pethā who married Prīmaladevī. She gave birth to three sons: Maṇḍana, Karmaṇa and Dharma. Their wifes were respectively Harṣū, Lalakū and Āsū. Prīmaladevī commissioned this manuscript, after her husband had listened to the teaching of Somasundarasūri, who was a pontiff of the Tapāgaccha. Somasundarasūri was born in V.S.1430 and became sūri in V.S. 1457. The counsellor Nārada copied this text in the year V.S. 1472.

MS-ADD-02377.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Jaina; Śvetāmbara, narrative. ; The story of the Jain monk Kālaka is one of the most famous legends and one of the most frequently illustrated Jain Śvetāmbara works. It is often appended to the Kalpasūtra , because both have a strong connection with the eight-day Jain festival of Paryuṣaṇ (August/September), which marks the climax of the rainy season. The ancient teacher Kālaka is held to be at the origin of the specific date where the last day of the festival takes place: the 4th day of the bright half of the month of Bhadrapada. The story is eventful and also shows how the Jain teacher took the help of a foreign king, the Sāhi, to restore the dharma and how he could use his magic abilities for this purpose. It is known from several different versions in Prakrit and Sanskrit. This manuscript has the most popular version of the story in Sanskrit. It is anonymous and known as Śrīvīravākyānumataṃ from its initial words. The manuscript has three typical, although not outstanding, illustrations.

MS-ADD-02418.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Kāvya; Alaṃkāraśāstra ; A manuscript of the Ghaṭakarparaṭīka , an unpublished commentary on the Ghaṭakarpara , a dūtakāvya or messenger poem. Allegedly, the poet is also known by the name Ghaṭakarpara, although n some traditional accounts and on the paper sleeve used as manuscript cover the poem is attributed to Kālidāsa. The poet famously employs the yamaka poetic device, 'paronomasia' or better 'cadence' (see Gerow 1977: 223-238), consistently in every stanza of the poem. The manuscript contains both the commentary and the poem, and the layout is in tripāṭha form. The commentary is attributed to Tārācandra (called Tārānātha on the paper sleeve). However, the text itself names him as being responsible for a revision of the commentary, and not necessarily as its author (see the explicit of the commentary under Excerpts; cf. also J. B. Chaudhuri 1953: 40); another possible interpretation is that the text in this manuscript is a revision, done by the author himself, of a previous version.

MS-ADD-02420.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Kāvya ; The Gaṅgālaharī , also known as Pīyūṣalaharī , is a well-known poem in 52 verses by Jagannātha Paṇḍita, a Sanskrit poet and scholar who thrived in the 17th century in the Mughal court of Śāh Jahān. Each verse of the poem is said to be one of the 52 steps that led to the river Ganges; according to the commentary by Sadāśiva, Jagannātha is said to have committed the fault of consorting with a yavana — in this context, a Muslim woman — and, desiring purification in the Ganges, composed these verses. As he recited each verse, it is said that the river rose one step. This paper manuscript is dated 1821 CE.

MS-ADD-02435.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Kāvya; Alaṅkāraśāstra ; This paper manuscript, dated 1618, is an early witness of the Rasataraṅgiṇī by Bhānudatta, son of the poet Gaṇapati, a renowned 16th-century treatise on aesthetic emotions ( rasa ), very influential in both Sanskrit and Hindi literary tradition from the 17th through the 19th century. From a theoretical viewpoint, Bhānudatta does not contribute any significant innovation to the theory of aesthetic emotions, but "his consumate skill in summarizing the thousand-year-long tradition of Indian aesthetic theory" and "his talent for crafting illustrative verses" are the most probable reason of his great fame, already within a few dacades of his death: for instance, "When Abu al-Fazl, the leading intellectual at the court of Akbar, presented a review of the arts and sciences of the Hindus to the Mughal emperor in the 1590s, he turned in part to the work of Bhanu to describe the nature of literature." (Pollock 2008: xix-xx)

Each exemplar is given a gloss that describes the different parts of the sentence. MS-ADD-02467.c: Manuscripts, Sanskrit; Vyākaraṇa; Alaṅkāraśāstra ; This paper manuscript contains the Māghakāvyadurghaṭa by Rājakuṇḍa (written Rājakruṃḍa in the manuscript), a commentary on the Śiśupālavadha of Māgha. The text consists of grammatical glosses of a few selected passages from each sarga of Māgha's 20- sarga poem.
