MS-KK-00003-00018.c: Great Britain. History. Anglo-Saxon period, 449-1066; Manuscripts, English (Old) ; Cambridge, University Library, MS Kk.3.18 (hereafter, MS Kk.3.18) is the youngest surviving copy of the Old English translation of Bede's Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum . Copied during the second half of the eleventh century at Worcester Cathedral Priory, MS Kk.3.18 played an important role in the use of English for pastoral care and preaching in Anglo-Norman England and beyond, as well as in the 'recovery' of Old English in the early modern period. Bede (673-735), a monk at Wearmouth-Jarrow, completed his Historia ecclesiastica in 731. It is the earliest surviving history of early England, from its mythic origins to the arrival and conversion of the Germanic tribes that eventually became the English, and the development of the early English Church. The Old English version of Bede's text was translated anonymously sometime around or before 900. This translation abridges its Latin source by about a third, cutting much of Bede's accounts of Roman Britain, various heresies and controversies, and most of the papal correspondence. MS-KK-00004-00025.c: Bestiary. Latin ; This manuscript is one of a small group of examples containing an uncommon textual recension. Minor variant readings of this manuscript prove that its text is the most faithful to that of the lost archetype among all the bestiary recensions. It is most similar to Cambridge, Fitzwilliam Museum, MS 254 in many aspects and was very probably copied from the same lost archetype. The main departures of Kk.4.25 from the Fitzwilliam bestiary are a slight change in the chapter order and the presence of two chapters of strictly didactic character that has no relation to the typical content of the bestiaries: Quattuor modis peccatum ('The Four Ways it is Sinful') and Quattuor colores caelestis ('The Four Heavenly Colours'). These two chapters appear after the chapter on the ibis. The first texts comes from Gregory the Great with some variations and paraphrases, while the second is a free paraphrase of Isidore of Seville's text on the rainbow ( arcus ). Both chapters appear in the cluster of content on birds, which was taken from a different textual version of the bestiary. MS-KK-00005-00006.e: Codex 3 + 69 + 4 Leaf height: 275-328 mm, width: 210-230 mm.
MS-KK-00005-00006.c: Music, Greek and Roman; Music theory History To 500 ; MS Kk.5.6 contains a treatise on music dating to about the 3rd century CE, De musica , written by Aristides Quintilianus . This work occupies the main part of the manuscript (part I, ff. [i]-[iii], 1-64, 70-74), and it was copied in the 16th century by a well-known scribe active in Italy, Camillo Zanetti (first half of the 16th century-after 1587). He also transcribed this same text on other occasions: for instance, in Venice in 1562, which copy is now Paris, Bibliothèque Nationale, MS gr. 2455 (see History, with refereneces). Another slightly later hand (hand B) added marginal annotations to Aristides Quintilianus' text, which are mostly collations from other manuscripts and critical notes. Furthermore, this hand traced a series of diagrams from another music treaty, Manuel Bryennius' Harmonica , on leaves that had been left blank by Zanetti. Hand B, moreover, wrote notes on Aristides Quintilianus' De musica in part II of the manuscript (ff. 65-69), which is a single quire of smaller paper leaves. These notes are written in Latin, and refer to passages in the text of MS Kk.5.6 (part I), using the pagination present on ff. 1r-55

MS-KK-00005-00007.c: Medicine, Greek and Roman ; Manuscript Kk.5.7 contains a single text, Erotian, Collection of Hippocratic words , a glossary of medical terms. Not much is known about this author, who lived in the 1st century CE, during the reign of emperor Nero. This copy of the text was made around the middle of the 16th century by the scribe Manuel Provataris (also known as Emmanuel Graecus). Born in Crete, Provataris was Scriptor at the Vatican Library from 1546-1571. Manuscript Kk.5.7 is currently bound as the second part of a single volume with three other manuscripts, Kk.5.6, 8 and 9. MS-KK-00005-00008.e: Codex 1 + 40 + 2, Leaf height: 330 mm, width: 215 mm.

The codex was probably copied in France, as the watermarks and the fact that it was owned by Jean-Baptiste Hautin suggest. The text was coped by a scribe who signed the copy of the last text in November 1592; although the colophon refers explicitly only to this text, since the rest of the manuscript has been written by the same scribe on the same kind of paper, the same period can be hypothesised for the copy af the whole manuscript. Manuscript Kk.5.6 is currently bound as the third part of a single volume with three other manuscripts, Kk.5.6, 7 and 9. Dr Erika Elia

MS-KK-00005-00009.c: Philosophy, Ancient ; Manuscript Kk.5.9 contains a small Greek philosophical miscellany comprising the commentary by Alexander of Aphrodias to books M and N of Aristotle's Metaphysics and a dialogue dealing with natural sciences by Theophylactus Simocatta (6th century CE), an author born in Egypt, best known for his historic work in eight books. All the texts here were copied in the 16th century by a well known scribe active in Italy, Camillo Zanetti (first half of the 16th century-after 1587; also known as Camillo Veneto). The commentary by Alexander of Aphrodias to books M and N, with the same lacuna at the end (see Contents), is found in other manuscripts copied by Camillo Zanetti, Oxford, Bodleian Library, Auct. T.1.17 (Misc. 195) and Oxford, Merton College, 304 (RGK I, 212), which was copied around 1581 in Padua from an exemplar owned by Gian Vincenzo Pinelli (see the description of the MS by N. Wilson in R.M. Thompson, A Descriptive Catalogue of the Medieval Manuscripts of Merton College, Oxford (2009), p. 268). Manuscript Kk.5.9 is currently bound as the fourth part of a single volume with three other manuscripts, Kk.5.6, 7 and 8. Dr Erika Elia

MS-KK-00005-00011.c: Synopsis Basilicorum ; The manuscript contains the Synopsis Basilicorum maior , an alphabetically arranged selection of the imperial laws, with the so-called Appendix A , a series of Novellae that often accompany this work. It was copied by the Greek scribe Nikolaos Tourrianos (1535/40-1608/10) in 1564 in Salamanca. Born in Crete, Tourrianos was active in various cities, such as Padua, Venice, Constantinople, Salamanca and Paris. He was scriptor of the University of Salamanca (1569-1573) and of the Library of El Escorial (from 1573). The exemplar of this codex, the first copied by Tourrianos in Spain (see de Andres 1969, p. 26), is MS El Escorial, Real Biblioteca, R.II.11 (see Easterling 1961, p. 259; Burgmann-Fögen-Schminck-Simon 1995, p. 59), owned by the Spanish humanist and diplomat Diego Hurtado de Mendoza: it was copied following a request by the jurist Eduardo Caldera. The Synopsis of the Basilics was really popular among Spanish jurists of the 16th century; after Diego Hurtado de Mendoza took one of his copies of the work to the Council of Trent, many copies of it were made. Nikolaos Tourrianos copied this work two more times, in MSS Salamanca, Biblioteca Universitaria, 273

MS-KK-00005-00012.e: Codex i + 168 + i Leaf height: 292 mm, width: 215 mm.
MS-KK-00005-00012.c: Greek language--Glossaries, vocabularies, etc. ; This manuscript, probably written in the 16th century, contains a simple Greek-Latin lexicon , arranged in two columns with Greek on the left and Latin on the right. In general the Latin supplies only a single synonym or occasionally a few alternatives or brief explanation of meaning, without citations or substantial commentary. The main lexicon is followed by a series of lists of Greek words whose gender differs from that of the Latin word designated as their equivalent. The Greek text has been written in full, but the Latin has been added only for the early part of the manuscript (to f. 57v ), probably at a later date. It appears not to match the intentions of the original copyist, since additional Greek words have been inserted into gaps left in the original Greek text, which at times appear somewhat out of alphabetical sequence, indicating that they were simply fitted in where space was available. It is not clear why these spaces had been left, but it could be that the Latin text corresponding to the words preceding them were expected to take up more space than the single half-line allowed for most entries. MS-KK-00005-00013.c: Agriculture ; What did monks at the Abbey of Saint-Denis like to eat a thousand years ago? What might they have grown in their cloister garden? And where did they learn about the right time to sow seeds or how to control garden pests? Answers to these questions lie within this 9th-century copy of De agricultura , a practical guide to estate management and farming techniques that was originally composed in the late 4th or early 5th century by Rutilius Taurus Aemilianus Palladius. The earliest extant manuscript that preserves the text of De agricultura in full, this manuscript is of outstanding importance for our understanding of the dissemination of the text. It belongs to the textual 'ɑ family', the version most prevalent among surviving manuscript witnesses. Text-critical analysis has shown that it preserves a form of the text close to that in the lost exemplar, 'ɑ', from which this family descended; it may even be a direct copy of it. MS-KK-00005-00016.t: Bede, Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum ('The Moore Bede')
MS-KK-00005-00016.e: Codex: iii + 128 + i leaves. Leaf height: 285 mm, width: 220 mm.
MS-KK-00005-00016.c: Great Britain. History. Anglo-Saxon period, 449-1066; Manuscripts, English (Old) ; Bede's Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum is the earliest surviving account of English history. Its central theme is the conversion of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms to Christianity and the establishment of the English Church. It was Bede's last major work; he finished writing it in 731, and died a few years later on 25 May 735. This manuscript is the earliest extant copy of Bede's history, and may well have been copied at his own monastery, at Wearmouth or Jarrow, within a few years of his death, perhaps as early as 737. It is usually called the 'The Moore Bede' because, prior to entering the collections of the University of Cambridge in 1715 as a gift from George I, it had been owned by John Moore, bishop of Ely (1707–1714). Moore had acquired it sometime between 1697 and 1702, and before that it had been in France, in the library of the cathedral of St. Julien at Le Mans. The ex libris of St. Julien can be seen at the foot of the last complete leaf (f. 128v ). Other evidence on that same page shows that the manuscript had been in France for a very long time, perhaps even since the reign of Charlemag

MS-KK-00005-00019.t: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War
MS-KK-00005-00019.d: second quarter of the 15th century and the year 1476
MS-KK-00005-00019.e: Codex9 + 309 + 9 Leaf height: 275 mm, width: 205 mm.
MS-KK-00005-00019.c: Greek literature; Thucydides; Thucydides. History of the Peloponnesian War ; This paper manuscript dating from the 15th century comprises a copy of Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War and three prefixed pieces concerning the work and life of the Athenian historian. The text of the History ends with an anonymous epigram in elegiac verses taken from the Palatine Anthology. The scribe of the manuscript has been identified as Demetrios Angelos, a Byzantine humanist and physician in the hospital of the Xenon of the Kral, in Constantinople. Angelos was among those scholars who chose to remain in the city following its capture by the Turks in May 1453 and thus did not take part in the important waves of migration to Italy. He is known to have purchased, gathered or copied numerous manuscripts and is thought to have been active from the second quarter of the 15th century as a pupil of Johannes Argyropulus (1416-1486) until 1476. The approximately thirty works he copied not only cover medicine and philosophy, but also history, in which he showed a profound interest. MS-KK-00005-00025.e: Codex iii + 267 + iii Leaf height: 300 mm, width: 190 mm.
MS-KK-00005-00025.c: Greek language--Glossaries, vocabularies, etc. ; This manuscript, produced in the late 15th century, contains the Lexicon of Pseudo-Zonaras , whose actual authorship is unknown, but which was traditionally attributed to the 12th-century Byzantine historian John Zonaras. Words to be defined are sorted into sections according to their first two letters, which are divided into subsections for masculine, feminine and neuter nouns, verbs and adverbs, but the entries are not alphabetically sorted beyond the first two letters. Some are glossed merely by giving a more common synonym, while others are accompanied by substantial paragraphs of discussion. At the end of the manuscript, the lexicon itself is followed by a number of entries which had been omitted from the text for some reason, and which are present in their normal alphabetical location in other manuscripts of this text. These are followed by a number of brief additional lexicographical lists, including glosses of unusual vocabulary from the Pauline Epistles, Hesiod and the Odyssey , words for the noises made by different animals, Egyptian names for the months, and brief excerpts from the poetry of the 12th-century writer Michael

MS-KK-00005-00026.t: Greek texts on music, mathematics and astronomy
MS-KK-00005-00026.e: Codex 2 + i + 181 + 2 Leaf height: 287 mm, width: 210 mm.
MS-KK-00005-00026.c: Mathematics, Greek Early works to 1800; Astronomy, Greek ; MS CUL Kk.5.26 is a miscellany containing Greek texts on music, mathematics and astronomy . The codex is a composite manuscript, formed of three parts. The first two (ff. 1-63) were copied in the first half of the 16th century, by Giovanni Onorio, scriptor and restaurator of the Vatican Library in the years 1535-1563, and by a contemporary hand. MS-KK-00005-00027.c: Philosophy, Ancient ; This manuscript contains the Commentary on the First Alcibiades , a dialogue traditionally attributed to Plato (but whose authorship is disputed), by Olympiodorus , teacher of philosophy in Alexandria in the 6th century CE. Olympiodorus' lectures, as transmitted by this commentary, were aimed to give an introduction to Plato. The codex, which was thought to be a late testimony of the text from the 17th century by its last editor (Westerink 1956, p. vii), can be traced back to the 16th century, after 1535. The watermark of the manuscript's paper is comparable with examples dated in the first half of the 16th century, and comes from a paper mill active in Troyes since 1503. The text derives from Paris, Bibliothèque Nationale de France, gr. 1822 , which was copied in 1535 in Venice by Angelos Bergikios, royal "scriptor" to the King of France in Fontainebleau (Westerink 1956, p. vii). An anononymous annotator, in a marginal note on f. 120v , seems to refer exactly to this exemplar. Therefore, the manuscript possibly originated in the French environment of Fontainebleau as well. Born in Crete, from 1539 he worked in Paris, where he was appointed by Francis I (1494-1547) scriptor of the Royal Library, which then was in Fontainebleau. MS-KK-00005-00037.c: Byzantine Empire--History ; This manuscript, dating to the later 16th century, contains the Byzantine chronicle of Constantine Manasses , quite unusual for a historical text in being written in verse. The author, a court poet and orator, composed the work at some point between 1145 and 1150. It was commissioned by the sebastokratorissa Eirene, the widowed sister-in-law of the Emperor Manuel I Komnenos (1118-1180, r. 1143-1180) and an important literary patron. Like many Byzantine chronicles, this text begins with the creation of the world, and it concludes with the reign of Nikephoros III Botaneiates (r. 1078-1081), the immediate predecessor of the reigning Komnenos dynasty. It appears to have been one of the most widely read of Byzantine historical works, surviving in 125 known copies and giving rise to a medieval Bulgarian translation and a 14th-century vernacular Greek paraphrase. This manuscript conforms to the standard format for copies of this text, including marginal notes helping the reader to navigate the text by identifying the emperor whose reign is being narrated and other indications of content. MS-KK-00006-00004.c: Bible ; This Acts and Epistles book was probably copied in the second half of the 10th century or first half of the 11th. The manuscript is a simple production with minimal ornament, and there was no supplementary textual content included apart from brief subscriptions at the end of most of the books, stating the context of the writing of each epistle and a conventional enumeration of the number of lines ( stichoi ). As was often the case with manuscripts not originally provided with such apparatus, later medieval users annotated it for liturgical use, marking out the lections to be read in the course of the liturgical calendar. In the first half of the 16th century the manuscript was owned by the French humanist François Vatable (Franciscus Vatablus) (d. 1547), a noted scholar of Hebrew as well as Greek, who was involved in efforts to produce an improved edition of the Bible. The author is unknown but has conventionally been referred to as Longinus or Pseudo-Longinus. On the Sublime is both a treatise on aesthetics and a work of literary criticism. It is also known for quoting (and thus transmitting) Sappho's fragment 31 (Φαίνεταί μοι). The codex is an autograph of the Italo-Cretan Hellenist Franciscus Portus (1511-1581; see Mazzucchi 1989, p. 216), who later edited the treatise ( Geneva 1569 ). In this edition, for instance, Sappho's text presents the corrections handed down from Kk.6.34 and the same colometry arrangement as on f. ii recto , due to Portus. MS-LC-II-00077.c: Benefactors ; This folio manuscript is Pembroke College’s Benefactors’ Book, a great work of seventeenth-century bibliography. Its largest section is an illustrated register of donors to Pembroke’s library, supplying the books that donors gave alongside their biographies and arms. It was begun in 1617 by Matthew Wren, uncle of the architect Christopher, who was Pembroke’s President at the time. Wren first listed all the previous gifts of books for which he could find evidence. Then he began entering gifts made to the library during his own tenure, of which the largest by far came from Lancelot Andrewes, Master of the College. (Have a look at his beautifully painted arms on f. 92r .) After Wren left Pembroke in 1624, other members of Pembroke continued making entries as new donations came in. This practice continued until the early eighteenth century. Nearly every seventeenth-century college in Oxford and Cambridge used a book like Wren’s to commemorate its library’s benefactors, following the lead of the Bodleian Library and All Souls College. Recto: after a history of abuse, a woman releases her husband, Abū l-ʿAlā, from all obligations to her in exchange for payment of 17 dinars. MS-LG-BIBLE-00002-00083.e: 1 leaf, part of a scroll. Leaf height: 53 cm, width: 38.5 cm.
MS-LG-BIBLE-00002-00083.c: Cairo Genizah ; Four columns of a Torah scroll, containing Leviticus 9:23-11:47. Although the top margin is lost, its original extent was 42 lines to a column. Columns and lines are ruled with a hard point. Sewing holes can be seen on the left-hand edge, which was the end of the yeriʿa. Tiberian vocalisation, including rafe, has been added at first sporadically, and then continually, to the text in column 4, which is also partially overwritten – probably as a writing exercise. The Tetragrammaton is written in a slightly different size of letters, or in a slightly different ink, indicating that it was probably originally left out of the writing of the scroll, and then filled in by the scribe when he was in the necessary state of purity. MS-LG-GLASS-00007.c: Cairo Genizah ; Sefer Josippon. The text on f. 1 contains the opening of chapter 54 (the fall of Antipater the wicked), lines 1-54, according to Flusser’s edition (1981). The text on f. 2 contains the end of chapter 55 (the death of Herod) and the beginning of chapter 56 (the days of Archelaus): ch. 55, lines 73-75, ch 56, lines 1-48, according to Flusser’s edition. On f. 1v, however, the text is arranged into two columns, successive numbered incipits appearing one below the other. On f. 2r the columnar approach is continued, though only the first third of the first column is required to complete the list. The final Psalm: הללו יה הללו אל (Psalm 150) is numbered as קמח. The opening Psalm on the list: מזמור לאסף (Psalm 73) is numbered as עא. MS-LG-GLASS-00023-A.e: 1 leaf + stub. Leaf height: 10.7 cm, width: 13.2 (1 leaf 11.7) cm.
MS-LG-GLASS-00023-A.c: Cairo Genizah ; Job 29:18-30:12. The fragment is from a high quality, single-column Masoretic codex, carefully produced, with plentiful Masora Parva and Magna. The layout is brick over brick, space over space, though the arrangement only sometimes corresponds with the semantics of the text. Orthographically, the text is close to that of the Aleppo Codex, though with some differences in matres lectionis. The vocalisation is standard Tiberian (though with a very few non-standard features, such as the inconsistent use of ḥaṭef qameṣ to indicate qameṣ ḥaṭuf). Occasionally, an expected dageš lene is omitted. Rafe is used consistently over spirantised begedkefat letters and non-consonantal final he. Where two spirantised begedkefat letters appear adjacent to one another, sometimes two rafe signs are used, and sometimes one centrally placed sign. Qere-Ketiv is indicated by a reversed final נ. The Masora Magna contains both elaborative and collative notes. The Aramaic parts (only) of the Masora Magna are marked with occasional Babylonian vowel signs. The Masora Magna notes are adorned with patterns made up from lines and circules. Ca. 11th-13th century.

MS-LG-GLASS-00024.e: holes, slightly stained. Leaf height: 18.8 cm, width: 13.8 cm.
MS-LG-GLASS-00024.c: Cairo Genizah ; Recto: Ezekiel 16:9-14. Verso: opens with the heading: וארא אל אברהם ביחזקאל, indicating that this is the hafṭara reading in Ezekiel for parašat va-ʾera (Exodus 6:2-9:35). Then follows Ezekiel 28:24-26. Ezekiel 16:9-14 is the latter part of the hafṭara reading for Exodus 1:1-6:1 (parašat šemot). The vocalisation of the readings contains various interesting features: (i) regular replacement of segol with pataḥ in the preformative of 1cs imperfect verbs, and sporadically in segolate noun forms; (ii) the almost total lack of ḥaṭef vowels in the document: these are replaced usually with a simple šewa, and sometimes with the equivalent full vowel; (iii) waw with a šewa preceding a labial consonant is vocalised as וְ rather than וּ; (iv) there is a vestige of the classical Tiberian pronunciation of šewa before a guttural in the vocalisation of לַעַבְדִּי. No formal Masora is presented as paratext to the biblical text itself, but two Qere-Ketiv notes are present. The consonantal text is close to that of the Aleppo Codex, though with some lapses. Rafe is used frequently over spirantised begadkefat letters. Gaʿya is not used. There are no cantillation signs. The rubric is wr

MS-LG-GLASS-00041.c: Cairo Genizah ; Isaiah 42:1-5. The Targum follows the Hebrew verse by verse. The Hebrew is vocalised with both Tiberian and simple Babylonian signs. The Tiberian vocalisation (which appears to be in the same ink as the consonantal text) is not quite full. The Targum is vocalised with Babylonian signs only. In addition to the basic Babylonian line system, the Babylonian dageš sign is frequently employed. Also, a distinct sign for segol (two dots above the consonant, leaning diagonally down to the left) is employed, though inconsistently.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00001.c: Cairo Genizah ; Seder ʿAvoda for Yom Kippur, containing the following elements. Recto: Piyyuṭ: בהיות אישים במזבח העולה, with א-ב acrostic; Piyyuṭ לא ארוחה להעמיד ארחינו, with double or triple line-internal א-ב acrostic; Piyyuṭ אשר אין מקדש לשרת כהן with א-ב acrostic; Piyyuṭ תלאה ורוש הקיפונו (part of the anonymous ʿAvoda אלהי קדם, also attested in Bodl MS Heb d.42 49b). Verso: Piyyuṭ כי אמרנו לרע טוב with א-ב acrostic; Piyyuṭ לא אמרתה לאבדינו with א-ב acrostic; Piyyuṭ או״א תתן אחרית לעמך (Mešullam b. Kalonymos); Toḵeḥa איום ונורא משפט יום בועירה with א-ב acrostic (first five lines only). Brief rubrics are interspersed between the poetic elements.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00006.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 20.6 cm, width: 16.7 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00006.c: Cairo Genizah ; Qedušta for Yom Kippur, attributed to Yannai. אהרן מעם נבחר. The first half of the poem (alphabetic acrostic; one strophe per letter) is preserved in T-S H5.199. The latter half, from the נ strophe, is preserved in this fragment. Thereafter, the first half of a second poem is preserved towards the bottom of the recto, and on the verso: אי עולם עת תתגאה לחדש ראשית (alphabetic acrostic; five strophes per letter). This poem is continued in T-S 18H1.5, in which the strophic structure of the poem is easier to determine.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00007.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 27.9 cm, width: 21.9 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00007.c: Cairo Genizah ; Yoṣerot for weekdays. Recto: most of the Yoṣer for Wednesday (incipit: וממנו אורים הצבתה); Yoṣer for Thursday, beginning בחמישי תנינים אידרתה, preceded by the title: יוצר אור יום חמישי; Yoṣer for Friday, beginning בשישי ארקה מילאתה, preceded by the title: יוצר אור יום השישי. Verso: three complete ברכות מזון, and the beginning of a fourth, each blessing with its own title. The latter two titles are almost entirely obliterated; the first two read: בירכת מזון דחולה; and בירכת מזון אבילים.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00008.e: 6 leaves (3 bifolia). Leaf height: 13.5 cm, width: 22.6 (1 leaf: 11.3) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00008.c: Cairo Genizah ; Liturgy for the weekday morning service with headings in larger letters (rubricated on f. 1r והוא, f. 4v אל and f. 6r א). The post-ʿAmida entreaty והוא רחום stretches (with only minor variations from the modern Ashkenazi rite) from the beginning of f. 1r, until half way down f. 4v. הטה begins on f. 1v; הבט נא begins on f. 2v; אנא מלך begins on f. 2v; אל רחום begins on f. 3r; אין כמוך begins on f. 3v; הפותח begins on f. 4r, and ends halfway down f. 4v. The rest of the text on f. 4v then continues directly with the אל ארך אפים section of the וידוי ויׄגׄ מידות. This continues until halfway down f. 5r. The rest of f. 5r, and the top of f. 5v repeat some of the הטה prayer. Then, halfway down f. 5v the opening prayer of the וידוי begins. Folio 6 is little more than a stub, and contains parts of Psalms 25 and 3. Folio 1r: incipit והוא רחום יכפר עון; explicit אדונינו אלהינו שׁמע קול תחנונינו. Folio 1v: incipit וזכר־לנו את־ברית אבותינו; explicit אל־תאחר: למענך. Folio 2r: incipit אלהי כי־שׁמך נקרא; explicit חננו ועננו כי לך ייי. Folio 2v: incipit עשׂה נפלאות בכל עת; explicit ומכל־צרה ויגון: הצילנו כי לך. Folio 3r: incipit תכלימנו והאר פניך; explicit אל תעזבנו אבינו ואל־תטשׁנו

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00009.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 12.8 cm, width: 10 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00009.c: Cairo Genizah ; Liturgy for the weekday morning service. The recto (incipit: צור חיינו) contains the מודים prayer from the conclusion of the ʿAmida, followed directly by the beginning of the ברכת כהנים, which continues onto the verso (incipit: יאר ייי פניו אליך). The שים שלום begins on line 2 of the verso, and אלהי נצור begins on line 10, and continues in a slightly smaller script.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00010.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 13.5 cm, width: 9.8 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00010.c: Cairo Genizah ; Liturgy for the weekday morning service with headings in larger letters. Recto: incipit מהרה יכרתון from the ʿAmida ברכת המינים. This is followed by על הצדיקים and ולירושלים. Verso: incipit תצמיח from the ʿAmida את־צמח דוד. This is followed by the רצה prayer, with the opening word רצה enlarged and rubricated, and by the opening of מודים (which continues directly on L-G Lit. 2.9r).

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00011.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 13.2 cm, width: 8.8 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00011.c: Cairo Genizah ; Liturgy for the weekday morning service: blessings from the ʿAmida. Recto: incipit חונן from אתה חונן. Followed by (a) השיבנו; (b) סלח לנו; (c) ראה בענינו; (d) רפאנו ייי. Verso: (a) ברך עלינו; (b) תקע בשופר; (c) השבה שופטינו; (d) the opening sentence of ולמלשינים (which continues directly on L-G Lit. 2.10).

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00012.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 13.7 cm, width: 9 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00012.c: Cairo Genizah ; Liturgy for the weekday morning service. Recto: the final portion of the גאל ישראל prayer from קריאת שמע (incipit: נאדר). This is followed by the opening of the ʿAmida; the word ברוך is enlarged and rubricated. Verso: the final part of the אתה גבור prayer, followed immediately by נקדש את שמך (the word נקדש is enlarged and rubricated), without the אתה קדוש ושמך קדוש prayer in between.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00013.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 13.4 cm, width: 11.7 (1 leaf: 6.9) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00013.c: Cairo Genizah ; Liturgy for the weekday morning service.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00014.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 19.3 cm, width: 26.8 (1 leaf 16.4) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00014.c: Cairo Genizah ; Fragments from three piyyuṭim. The first is an alphabetic acrostic with the ט to ת strophes preserved: ‏[מלך טוב] ומטיב לכול פועל ואין כמוהו מלך. מלך יחיד יושב בשמים ואין כמוהו מלך. Of the second, only the first line is preserved at the bottom of f. 1v: מלך רחום שמו פארוהו. F. 2 contains strophes ט to ע of a piyyuṭ, presumably for Sukkot. The final phrase of each strophe contains a sequential citation from Leviticus 23:40–41, such that when these phrases are read together they give the full citation of the biblical text. Incipit: ביזכור שבעת הימים יום וליל לחלותך.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00015.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 18.7 cm, width: 16.4 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00015.c: Cairo Genizah ; Liturgy for the weekday morning service. Incipit: ‏[מאר]בע כנפות הארץ from the final part of the אהבה רבה prayer, from the קריאת שמע section of the liturgy. The שמע itself is summarised thus: שמע ישר כליה. This is followed by the full text of אמת ויציב, על הראשונים, עזרת אבותינו, with the opening of the ʿAmida on the bottom four lines of the verso. The text closely follows the modern Ashkenazi wording, though with numerous small omissions, inversions, and additions. Frequently, common words and phrases are abbreviated to their first consonant.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00016.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 8.8 cm, width: 8.1 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00016.c: Cairo Genizah ; A fragment from an unknown piyyuṭ. Incipit: ‏[...]אר גאה ולבבות הכאה.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00017.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 15.5 cm, width: 26 (1 leaf: 13) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00017.c: Cairo Genizah ; A collection of piyyuṭim. F. 1r: ‏[הא]דיר בגבהי שמים. Alphabetic acrostic; strophes ט to צ have been omitted. The rhyme throughout is the syllable קים. This is followed by the rubric: ובכן תתפאר אש קדש, which introduces a fourfold תשר׳׳ק piyyuṭ, incipit: ‏[...]ת: כי לך התהלה. Only strophes ת to מ are provided, continuing onto f. 1v. F. 1v continues with the rubric: ובכן יתקדש שמך יי אלהינו, introducing an alphabetic acrostic, incipit: יתקדש אדון כל הארץ מרום וקדוש הוא יתקדש. The clause מרום וקדוש הוא יתקדש is repeated as a refrain, and is frequently abbreviated to just the first couple of letters of each word. F. 2 contains sections from the Seder ͑Avoda for Yom Kippur. Incipit: שנ׳ ברכה, שנ׳ גאולה, שנ׳ דרור from the high priest’s prayer on leaving the Holy of Holies.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00018.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 24.7 cm, width: 43.5 (1 leaf: 21.8) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00018.c: Cairo Genizah ; Parts of three piyyuṭim by Yannai. F. 1r: incipit תקום תקים from a Qedušta for the Šabbat of Ḥanukka, which continues onto f. 1v. Followed by a Šivʿata for Parašat Šeqalim: כי תשא את ראש אהובים, which continues onto f. 2r. The rest of f. 2 contains a Qedušta for Parašat Šeqalim: אותיות הבאות שרתה.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00019.e: 1 leaf + stub. Leaf height: 16.2 cm, width: 18.7 (1 leaf: 15.7) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00019.c: Cairo Genizah ; Recto: part of an Aramaic alphabetic acrostic piyyuṭ for Purim. Incipit: ושליט המן. At the bottom of the recto, and onto the verso, the havdala blessings are written in a semi-cursive hand. The text of the blessings is much abbreviated, usually giving only the first letter of each word. This is followed, half way down the verso, by part of the prayer before sleep המלאך הגואל אותי. The final third of the verso contains abbreviated forms of biblical verses containing the word שלום: Numbers 25:12; Leviticus 26:6; 1 Chronicles 12:14; Isaiah 27:5; Psalm 85:9-11.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00020.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 11.1 cm, width: 24.2 (1 leaf: 12.1) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00020.c: Cairo Genizah ; Šivʿatot for Sabbaths, by R. Ḥaduta b. Abraham. F.1r: incipit: עם לא אלמן, half way through the poem for the מגן blessing. The seventh poem begins on the final line of f. 1v, and continues directly onto ENA 2132.17-18. The first word of each of the seven poems forms an alphabetic acrostic א to ז. F. 2r: incipit: דשנינו בשביתת from the poem for the מגן blessing in the Šivʿata אתן מאז ניתבחר לך. The beginning of the poem is preserved in ENA 2132.17-18. The Šivʿata continues onto f. 2v, up to the first line of the sixth poem.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00021.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 18.4 cm, width: 29.8 (1 leaf: 14.9) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00021.c: Cairo Genizah ; Hošʿanot. (1) F. 1r, incipit: למ׳ משרת פי. Double acrostic, with strophes מ to ת preserved. The end of the piyyuṭ is indicated by a circellus, and the next piyyuṭ is marked with the heading הושענה.‎ (2) A single-strophe alphabetic Hošʿana, beginning on the pre-penultimate line of f. 1r; incipit: למען אב שני נעריו קח. It concludes at the bottom of f. 1v. An omitted line was added in the left hand margin of f. 1v, in a different hand to that of the main text. (3) A new Hošʿana, with תשר’’ק pattern, begins at the top of f. 2r; incipit: למענך תקיף במעונה. The opening lines, up to the פ strophe, are very similar to a Hošʿana appearing in Saadia’s siddur. (4) A fourth, single-strophe alphabetic, Hošʿana begins at the bottom of f. 2r; incipit: ענה אום שר מראש אמנה, and continues until half way down f. 2v. (5) The opening strophes, from ת to פ of a תשר׳׳ק piyyuṭ; incipit: תומים בני אמי.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00022.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 9.9 cm, width: 14.4 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00022.c: Cairo Genizah ; Yoṣerot for Šabbat Zeḵor. (a) Rešut. Heading: ויהי; acrostic: יוסף. Incipit: יהי אור אמר וכל כל בחכמה.‎ (b) Yoṣer. Heading: יוצר לזכור; acrostic: א’’ב. Incipit: אזכיר שטמת אויב דולק. Phrases from Deuteronomy 25:17-19 appear throughout the poem ‎(c) Heading: אחר. Each section of the poem opens with the first word(s) of each verse from Leviticus 1:1-4: ויקרא… דבר… [אם]...וסמך ידו. Each section closes with a citation from Deuteronomy 25:17-18.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00023.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 30.4 cm, width: 18.4 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00023.c: Cairo Genizah ; Seliḥa. (a) A Ḥaṭanu, with the refrain חטאנו occurring seven times throughout the poem, which concludes on f. 2v. Incipit: אתנפל ואתודה בתחנונים לפניך אל נורא ואיום. (b) A list of פזמונים (abbreviated to פי), each of which begins with the divine name (which is itself abbreviated to יי with a flourish).

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00024.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 16.9 cm, width: 13.6 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00024.c: Cairo Genizah ; Šabbat service: ʿAmida, with very similar wording to Saʿadya’s Siddur. The fragment contains the latter part of the מקדש השבת blessing for the Musaf service, followed by the wording of the same blessing for the Minḥa service. See Davidson’s edition of Saʿadya’s Siddur, 111-113. The fragment closes with the first part of the וצדקתך collection of biblical verses (see Siddur RaSaG, 122).

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00025.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 9.7 cm, width: 14.5 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00025.c: Cairo Genizah ; Yoṣerot for Šabbat Zeḵor. (1) The final part of a Silluq. Acrostic: ‏(י?)עקב. Incipit: ובשלשתם הם נכונים.‎ Concludes with Isaiah 6:3: וקרא זה אל זה ואמר ק ק ק.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00026.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 17.1 cm, width: 14.4 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00026.c: Cairo Genizah ; Qinot for the Ninth of Av, by Elʿazar b. Qallir. (a) The latter part of איכה תפארתי מראשותי השליכו, beginning midway through the פ strophe. Incipit: מי תחלה. An alphabetic acrostic. The first word of each strophe is the same as the first word of each verse in Lamentations 2. The biblical citations at the end of each strophe are taken from Leviticus 26. (b) The first part of איכה אשפתו פתוח כקבר, up to the beginning of the ה strophe. This alphabetic acrostic is built on the opening words of each verse of Lamentations 1, 3 and 5.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00027.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 17.7 cm, width: 25.7 (1 leaf: 12.9) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00027.c: Cairo Genizah ; Passover Haggada, very closely based on Saʿadya’s version. (a) Incipit: מאידה עליהא בקול והליק (the rubric preceding the בורא פרי האדמה blessing; (b) מה נשתנה; (c) עבדים היינו - incomplete: the text ends part way through the רשע מה הוא אומר section. The vocalisation of the Hebrew is largely Tiberian, though with occasional interchange of pataḥ and qameṣ, and pataḥ and segol. The relative particle ש is consistently vocalised with pataḥ, and the infinitive לשאל is vocalised with pataḥ rather than ḥolem.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00028.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 12.3 cm, width: 23 (1 leaf: 12.3) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00028.c: Cairo Genizah ; Piyyuṭim for Birkat ha-Mazon, in particular for Passover, Šemini ʿAṣeret, Sukkot and Roš ha-Šana. Folio 1r: (a) heading ברכת פסח; incipit: אז בפסח גאלתה. (b) heading ברכת עצרת; incipit: בסיניי איזנתנו אות מידך. This continues onto 1v, and is followed by: (c) heading ברכת ראש השנה; incipit: אומץ יום תרועה; this blessing continues onto L-G Lit. 2.42 f. 1r. Folio 2r: (a) incipit שלום משקיף משמי מעונים. (b) heading ברכה לסוכה; incipit: אוגדי ריבוע סיחים. This continues onto 2v and is followed by: (c) heading: ברכת פסח; incipit: אברך לנורא עלילה.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00029.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 14.5 cm, width: 11.9 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00029.c: Cairo Genizah ; Small fragment of a widely spaced ketubba for the groom Isaac b. Ḥalfon, in Cairo, with a heading in larger letters. The extant text reads: יצליחו: ... תין וחמשה שנין למנינינו דרגיליננא ביה באלקאהרה ... דוד יצח ... בחור היקר חתנא בר כגק מר̇ור̇ ... חלפ ... ישראל.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00030.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 15 cm, width: 32.4 (1 leaf: 16.2) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00030.c: Cairo Genizah ; Piyyuṭim. Folio 1 contains piyyuṭim for morning prayers. Folio 1r opens with (a) the last two lines of what may be an ’Ofan, concluding: ודמות פניהם פני אדם; (b) heading: מאורות, incipit: ידך תרומם דבירך לקומם. Each stanza consists of four short lines. The first letters of each stanza spell out יהודה. The first three lines of each stanza share a rhyme, while the final line of each stanza ends with the rhyme syllable לים. Folio 1v: heading ברוך שאמר, incipit: ברוך אשר שפרר שקופי שפי שלבי שפרת שמי שבעת שחקים והתלילם. Folio 2 contains part of an alphabetic Azhara. Each letter seems to begin five lines. The letters ס to צ are preserved.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00031.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 11.3 cm, width: 16.5 (1 leaf: 8.3) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00031.c: Cairo Genizah ; Liturgy for weekday morning prayers. Folio 1 contains part of the post-‘Amida Taḥanun והוא רחום (most of the אין כמוך חנון ורחום, and the first part of the הפותח יד). Incipit: וליעקב אל תפן אל קשינו. Explicit: אם אין בנו צדקה ומעשים טובים זכור לנו את. Folio 2 contains part of the Qeri’at Ha-Tora section of the morning service (sections from the הוצאת ספר תורה and the קריאת התורה, though with substantial differences to the Ashkenazi Siddur). Folio 2r contains (a) a version of the prayer אל ארך אפים. The אל is written in large script; (b) the liturgical instruction (in Hebrew): ומוציא ספר תורה ואמ̇, followed immediately by the גדלו לייי אתי (the first word is written in large script). This continues onto folio 2v, and is followed by (c) the liturgical instruction (in Hebrew): ועולה ספר תורה לתיבה, and (d) a form of the half-Qaddiš: על הכל יתגדל ויתקדש (the first word is written in large script).

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00032.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 14.3 cm, width: 19.8 (1 leaf: 10) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00032.c: Cairo Genizah ; Prayers for Yom Kippur. F. 1r: incipit מושל[ים ...]רים באלהים בקולם ילעיגו לנו. F. 1v: the prayer הנשמה לך is immediately followed by Solomon ibn Gabirol’s אז בחשבי למרחוק, followed by the הנשמה לך refrain. F. 2: part of the Yom Kippur viddui. The folio opens with the last few repetitions of the ועל חטא שחטאנו לפניך prayer, followed by the ועל חטאים שאנו חיבים עליהם. F. 2v ends with וזרקתי עליכם מים טהורים וטהרתם מכל טמאותיכם ומכל גלוליכם אטהר אתכם.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00033.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 14.2 cm, width: 19.5 (1 leaf: 9.8) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00033.c: Cairo Genizah ; Piyyuṭim for Purim. (1) Alphabetic acrostic poem, where each successive stanza begins with the next letter of the alphabet. The piyyuṭ sequentially lists the many enemies of Israel from the Bible. F. 1r contains strophes ט to מ; f. 1v contains strophes מ to ע; f. 2r contains strophes פ to ר; f. 2v contains strophes ר to ת. The refrain consists of (at least) the first verse of Psalm 3 (יי מה רבו צרי רבים קמים עלי) followed by: והמן עוד בא: לאבדי בהתיעצו: ונתלה על עצו: כן יאבדו כל אויב[י] יי. A final stanza after the alphabetic acrostic contains the acrostic פינחשׂ (sic.) The first part of the poem (strophes א to ח) is preserved in L-G Lit. 2.46. (2) At the bottom of f. 2v the first four lines of another alphabetic acrostic are preserved, beginning: אבד תאבד אלופי אדום.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00034.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 22.7 cm, width: 16 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00034.c: Cairo Genizah ; Musaf for Roš ha-Šana. Recto: the final few lines of זכרונות. Incipit: כבש רחמיו לעשות רצוך (sic.). This is followed immediately by שופרות. Of many of the longer biblical citations only the opening phrases are written, usually followed by וג. Verso: part of the Passover Haggada. Incipit: ברוך אתה יי...בורא פרי הגפן, followed by מה נשתנה and עבדים היינו.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00035.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 17.4 cm, width: 15 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00035.c: Cairo Genizah ; Part of a ketubba for Ḡālib b. Solomon ha-Levi and Jamīla bat ʿEli, in the handwriting of Abraham b. Natan, Av Bet Din. 11th-12th century.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00036.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 23 cm, width: 24.1 (1 leaf: 15.4) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00036.c: Cairo Genizah ; Fragment from a bifolium containing yoṣerot by Elʿazar b. Qallir. F. 1 is a stub. Most of this leaf is conserved under classmark L-G Lit. 2.45. F. 1 contains an alphabetic acrostic piyyuṭ for parašat כי תשא, which concludes at the bottom of f. 1v. This is followed by the opening words of another for the same paraša, which continues onto f. 2. F. 2r (incipit: הטוב: טוב שמן) contains the latter part of an alphabetic acrostic piyyuṭ for parašat כי תשא, and the beginning of another for parašat ויקהל, which continues onto, and fills, f. 2v.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00037.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 11.6 cm, width: 22.5 (1 leaf: 11.2) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00037.c: Cairo Genizah ; Leaf from a Passover Haggada. (a) F. 1r: a colophon giving the owner's name, Hiba b. Yefet al-Ḡazzī: האדה אלקדוס לחבה ביר יפת אלגזי ס’’ט יחייהו וישמרהו. (b) F. 1v: The qidduš opening the Passover Haggada, with the heading: בשמך רחמנא קידוס ללפסח. The wording of the qidduš is a heavily abridged form of that found in Saʿadya’s Siddur (see Davidson edition, p. 141). (c) F. 2: Psalms 113 and 114 from the half-Hallel, followed by the גאל ישראל blessing, which concludes at the bottom of f. 2v.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00039.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 24.4 cm, width: 15.6 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00039.c: Cairo Genizah ; Babylonian Talmud, Šabbat 71b-74a. Incipit: אבל קודם הפרשה. Explicit: אלא א’ רב המנונא.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00040.e: 2 leaves conjoined (bifolium). Leaf height: 17.2 cm, width: 26 (1 leaf: 14.9) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00040.c: Cairo Genizah ; Qinot for the Ninth of Av, from Siddur Saʿadya Gaʾon. F. 1r (incipit: חשך ואפלה - end of the צ strophe) contains the latter part of the qina איליל הה ליום המפרק גדילים, followed by אבוי לירח חמישי, which continues onto f. 1v. F.1v continues with אויה לי כי נלטשו נסכנות, up to the beginning of the צ strophe. F. 2r contains the last part of אני הגבר מנעורי (from the end of the ע strophe onwards), followed by איכה רחובות עיר, which continues onto f. 2v. F. 2v ends with the first few lines of זכור תבוסת צאן טבחה (up to midway through the ר strophe). The text contains a few variants (usually spelling) when compared to Davidson’s edition of Saʿadya's Siddur.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00041.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 11.9 cm, width: 19 (1 leaf: 16) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00041.c: Cairo Genizah ; Raḥamin. A collection of biblical verses entreating divine mercy and deliverance. Similar to the collection found in Saʿadya’s siddur. On f. 1r most of the verses include the root בטח; on f. 1v most of the verses include the root ישע.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00042.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 13 cm, width: 25.4 (1 leaf: 13.5) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00042.c: Cairo Genizah ; Piyyuṭim for Birkat ha-Mazon, in particular for Sukkot and Roš ha-Šana.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00043.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 14.3 cm, width: 16 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00043.c: Cairo Genizah ; Qedušta by Elʿazar b. Qallir: אומן שלא קם כמותו. The fragment contains a section from the seventh part (the silluq in this case) of the qedušta. The silluq begins: מי גבר יחיה ולא יראה מות. The scribe has divided the silluq into sections: in the section beginning ואז כפץ צור לעניו the first word is written in large letters (recto). Likewise, in the section of the poem beginning והוא משיב לבת קול ואומר, the first word is written in large letters (verso). Incipit: עמלו ואחריתו. Explicit: ירד אשר.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00044.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 40.3 cm, width: 7 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00044.c: Cairo Genizah ; List of 30 piyyuṭim on a long tapered piece of vellum, referenced according to the first few words of their opening lines. Four are well known piyyuṭim by Solomon Ibn Gabirol, such as the poem שוכני בתי חומר, or the seliḥa שחר קמתי להודות. Seven poems by Isaac ibn Ḡiyyāṯ also appear on the list, such as יום ערום אעמוד (part of the qerova for the morning service of Yom Kippur). The list also contains two works by Joseph Ibn Abitur and one by Ḥasday Ibn Šapruṭ, as well as various anonymous titles.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00045.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 22.1 cm, width: 10.6 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00045.c: Cairo Genizah ; Half a leaf from a collection of yoṣerot by Elʿazar b. Qallir. The fragment is from the same leaf as the stub (folio 1) preserved in L-G Lit. 2.36. It contains the latter part of a piyyuṭ for parašat תצוה, followed by a piyyuṭ for parašat כי תשא (beginning: אהובים נוחלי זכור ושמור).

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00046.e: 1 leaf + stub. Leaf height: 14.4 cm, width: 10.5 (1 leaf: 9.7) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00046.c: Cairo Genizah ; Piyyuṭim for Purim. (1) Strophes א to ח of an alphabetic acrostic poem, where each successive stanza begins with the next letter of the alphabet. The piyyuṭ sequentially lists the many enemies of Israel from the Bible. The refrain consists of (at least) the first verse of Psalm 3 (יי מה רבו צרי רבים קמים עלי) followed by: והמן עוד בא: לאבדי בהתיעצו: ונתלה על עצו: כן יאבדו כל אויב[י] יי. A final stanza after the alphabetic acrostic contains the acrostic פינחשׂ (sic.) The rest of the poem is preserved in L-G Lit. 2.33.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00047.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 7.4 cm, width: 14.5 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00047.c: Cairo Genizah ; From the ʿArvit (evening service) version of the Qeriʾat Šemaʿ. Recto: incipit: על מזזות ביתך ובשעריך. Explicit: יורה ומלקוש. Verso: incipit: בני ישראל ואמרת אלהם ועשו להם ציצת. Explicit: ועשיתם אתם ולא.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00050.e: 1 leaf + stub. Leaf height: 13 cm, width: 15.8 (1 leaf: 12.8) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00050.c: Cairo Genizah ; (a) The recto begins with the continuation of a seliḥa that began on L-G Lit. 2.42 f. 1v. This is followed by the first lines of various biblical תפלות (perhaps intended as aides memoire for the recitation of the whole Psalm: תפלה למשה (Psalm 90); תפלה לעני (Psalm 102); תפלה לחבקוק (Habakkuk 3). This is followed by (b) An Arabic text (in Arabic characters) on the pharmacological preparation of various materials via boiling and evaporation. Verso (a) heading: ברכת חודש. A piyyuṭ for Birkat ha-Mazon, in particular for Roš ḥodeš.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00052.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 10.5 cm, width: 18.2 (1 leaf: 9.1) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00052.c: Cairo Genizah ; F. 1: Esther 1:1-4a, with pen trials and writing exercises in the margins. F. 2: Instructions, in Judaeo-Arabic, regarding liturgical requirements when Passover falls on the evening of Šabbat. Children’s jottings appear in the margins, including a drawing of a lion-like creature on f. 2r.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00054.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 14.3 cm, width: 22 (1 leaf: 11) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00054.c: Cairo Genizah ; Folio 1r: part of the Birkat ha-Mazon הטוב והמטיב (though with many differences from the modern Ashkenazi form and wording). Folio 1v: blank. Folio 2v: blank. Folio 2r: a poetic form of the first blessing of Birkat ha-Mazon, written in a very unaccomplished hand. The first line appears to be a heading containing the Judaeo-Arabic rubric: ויקול. The ברוך אתה introduction is abbreviated to a single ligature. The main text of the blessing reads:

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00057.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 16.2 cm, width: 12.1 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00057.c: Cairo Genizah ; Passover Haggada. Incipit: הנהר ואולך from the section: מתחלה עובדי עבודה זרה היו אבותינו. After the words ועבדום וענו אתם ארבע מאות שנה the text continues, without break, to the words: ויוצאנו ייי ממצרים לא על־ידי מלאך. The vocalisation deviates from Standard Tiberian in several ways: full vowels are sometimes used instead of ḥaṭef; gemination is sometimes omitted; there is interchange of pataḥ and segol in the environment of gutturals.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00066.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 18.3 cm, width: 13.7 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00066.c: Cairo Genizah ; Passover Haggada. Incipit: וירעו אתנו המצרים from the section ארמי אבד אבי. The text continues up to the beginning of the description of the ten plagues. On the recto, the beginning of each new text unit is marked by the use of a large, formal square script, rather than the informal, semi-square script in which the rest of the text is written.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00068.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 13.4 cm, width: 9.4 cm.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00093.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 16.2 cm, width: 8.7 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00093.c: Cairo Genizah ; Passover Haggada. From the אשר גאלנו section of the Haggada. Recto; incipit: יגיענו לרגלים, followed by the פרי הגפן and נטילת ידים blessings. Verso: the מוציא, מצה, מרור blessings. The instructions are given in Judaeo-Arabic.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00097.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 18.9 cm, width: 14.2 cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00097.c: Cairo Genizah ; Psalms 8:1-9:21. The text is written in an accomplished semi-cursive hand, and is unvocalised and uncantillated. Nonetheless, the orthography closely follows the MT. Unusually, the tetragrammaton is written out in full. The fragment contains a number of lapsus calami; the most prominent occurs at 9:14-15 in which six words have been omitted by parablepsis. The final two lines of Psalm 9 have been written transversely in the right hand vertical margin. This, and the fact that Psalm 8 begins at the very top of the recto, may suggest that the leaf was only ever intended to contain these two Psalms.

MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00162.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 13 cm, width: 17 (1 leaf: 8.5) cm.
MS-LG-LITURGY-00002-00162.c: Cairo Genizah ; Part of an anonymous qerova for the Eighteen Benedictions. One stanza is allocated per blessing. Each stanza is built around short lemmata from three consecutive verses from Song of Songs 1. Folio 1r contains the last line of the stanza for the מחייה המתים blessing, followed by the stanzas for האל הקדוש and חונן דעת. Folio 1v contains the stanzas for הרוצה בתשובה and the first half of the stanza for המרבה לסלוח. The text breaks off halfway down f.1v. Folio 2 is blank.

MS-LG-MISC-00001.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 39.9 cm, width: 28.4 cm.
MS-LG-MISC-00001.c: Cairo Genizah ; Leaf from a Hebrew treatise on the composition of various drugs. The fragment opens with a chapter on cancer, including treatments with different kinds of clay (i.e. Armenian clay), followed by sections on abscesses, flatulence, and arteries. On verso, a new chapter (the third) on leprosy begins. The treatise appears to be derived from an Arabic original since the word for ‘maiming’ is first reported in transliteration from Arabic and then in Hebrew translation (גדמות).

MS-LG-MISC-00002.c: Cairo Genizah ; Ketubba for an unknown bride and groom. A line on verso mentions ‘our lord Isaac’, and amounts of money are given in dinars and dirhams. Probably in the hand of Nathan b. Solomon (active 1125-1150 CE).

MS-LG-MISC-00003.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 12.8 cm, width: 15 cm.
MS-LG-MISC-00003.c: Cairo Genizah ; Halakhic work relating to inheritance and women.

MS-LG-MISC-00005.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 31.7 cm, width: 18.3 cm.

MS-LG-MISC-00009.c: Cairo Genizah ; Instructions from Joseph b. Abraham b. Bundār in Aden, directing his agent Isḥāq Nafūsī to purchase and sell certain goods. Refers to Dammūh, (Elʿazar Ibn) al-Qaṣabī, and (Ḥalfon b. Manasseh Ibn) al-Qaṭāʾif. Ca. 1130 CE.

MS-LG-MISC-00010.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 18 cm, width: 13.1 cm.
MS-LG-MISC-00010.c: Cairo Genizah ; Part of a letter from the Yeshiva of Gaʾon Samuel b. ʿEli (in Baghdad), with opening praises.

MS-LG-MISC-00011.c: Cairo Genizah ; Letter from the Yeshiva of Gaʾon Samuel b. ʿEli (in Baghdad), sent to a community regarding an on-going discussion about women married against their will (i.e. captives), and also referring to government edicts about marriage (i.e. non-Jewish marriage).

MS-LG-MISC-00012.e: 3 leaves. Leaf height: 4.6 cm, width: 8.9 cm.
MS-LG-MISC-00012.c: Cairo Genizah ; The first fragment under this classmark is a letter to Elijah b. Zechariah the judge from Nissim, addressing Elijah and his son Zechariah the doctor (Abū Zikrī). Ca. early 13th century. The second fragment contains Arabic jottings and Coptic numerals.

MS-LG-MISC-00013.c: Cairo Genizah ; Letter from Isaac b. Aaron al-Sijilmāsī in Dahlak to Ḥalfon b. Nathaniel ha-Levi, reporting lives lost at sea. Mentions a great number of names, including Abū l-Ḵayr al-Najjār (‘the carpenter’), Ibn al-Šumūs, David, Ibn Zuġmār, Ibn al-Raqqāṣa, Abū Naṣr, Abū l-Faraj, and Abū l-Barakāt. Ca. mid-12th century.

MS-LG-MISC-00016.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 12.7 cm, width: 16.7 (1 leaf: 8.3) cm.

Includes two magical formulae made up of repetitions of single letters, of a pair of letters, and of syllables from the name of God. The pages are numbered and (ד) appears at the top right corner of f. 1v. Sections of text are enclosed in frames on f. 1v (lines 12-16) and f. 2v (lines 7-13).

au: Ḥusn bat Yaḥyā Ibn al-Zūrīqā (wife of Solomon Abū Naṣr b. Saʿadya b. Hallūn)

MS-LG-MISC-00020.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 7.7 cm, width: 8.9 cm.

MS-LG-MISC-00021.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 5.2 cm, width: 9.7 cm.

MS-LG-MISC-00022.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 4.3 cm, width: 6.5 cm.
MS-LG-MISC-00022.c: Cairo Genizah ; Very small fragment, probably from a prayer book.

MS-LG-MISC-00023.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 18.4 cm, width: 19 cm.
MS-LG-MISC-00023.c: Cairo Genizah ; Legal documents in the hand of Ḥalfon b. Manasseh. Recto: after a history of abuse, a woman releases her husband, Abū l-ʿAlā, from all obligations to her in exchange for payment of 17 dinars. The formulae cover all possible future scenarios such as divorce, and the death of either party. Her children, Abū l-Ḵayr and Sitt al-Kull, are also mentioned. Verso: legal document concerning a debt resulting from the sale of a house; the parties being Nissan Abū Saʿd and Abū l-ʿAlā (possibly the same individual on recto). Written in Fusṭāṭ under the authority of Maṣliaḥ ha-Kohen, dated 14[4]1 of the Seleucid Era (= 1130 CE). Signed by Manasseh ha-Kohen b. Jacob and Ḥalfon b. Manasseh.

MS-LG-MISC-00024.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 22.6 cm, width: 33.4 cm.

MS-LG-MISC-00033.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 13.5 cm, width: 10.1 cm.
MS-LG-MISC-00033.c: Cairo Genizah ; Recto: draft of a legal document with the testimony of Abū l-Ḵayr. Mentions Ephraim b. Sason, Judah b. [...], Abū Kaṯīr and [... b.] ʿIzrūn. Verso: probably a (draft) letter concerning business matters. Ca. late 11th century or early 12th century.

MS-LG-MISC-00034.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 27.5 cm, width: 20.5 cm.
MS-LG-MISC-00034.c: Cairo Genizah ; Begging letter from ‘a man from the people of Qayrawān’, describing how he came to Fusṭāṭ in order to get financial support from his relative Nahray (b. Nissim, active 1060-1097 CE). The writer had also turned for help to Abū Zikrī, which incurred the wrath of Nahray, and the writer promised henceforth to rely only on Nahray. But since then Nahray has only paid him the insufficient sum of 15 dirhams over the course of eight months. Now the writer is too ashamed to address Abū Zikrī, and he has therefore written this note to a third potential patron to solicit support.

MS-LG-MISC-00035.e: 1 leaf. Leaf height: 13.5 cm, width: 10.1 cm.
MS-LG-MISC-00035.c: Cairo Genizah ; Letter from a Jewish woman who has suffered at the hands of the invading Seljuk Turks in the 1070s CE. She had to flee from Jerusalem to Tripoli in the Lebanon, where she reports on the carnage she witnessed: ‘I was with him on the day I saw them killed in terrible fashion... I am an ill woman on the brink of insanity, on top of the hunger of my family and the little girl who are all with me, and the horrid news I heard about my son.’ She suggests it would be better to be captured since those in captivity ‘find someone who gives them food and drink’, whereas uncaptured, she and her children are starving.

MS-LG-MISC-00042.e: 2 leaves (bifolium). Leaf height: 16.8 cm, width: 24.5 (12.5) cm.
MS-LG-MISC-00042.c: Cairo Genizah ; Legal document for the engagement of Ṭoviyya b. Tiqva and Sitt al-Kull bat Peraḥya, witnessed by Abraham b. Šemaʿya he-Ḥaver, Isaac b. Samuel ha-Sefardi and Ḥalfon b. Manasseh. Dated Kislev 1431 of the Seleucid Era (= 1119 CE). It is in fact the earliest known example of such a deed, since formalising a couple’s engagement with a legal document appears to have been an innovation of the 12th century. Jewish marriage is a three-stage process: engagement, betrothal and marriage. Betrothal, at which the couple are declared married but do not move in together, and marriage, when the woman leaves her father’s house and lives with her husband, are both formal events requiring a written document. Engagement, however, was an oral agreement of a more informal nature. In 12th-century Fustat, Egypt, however, the Jewish community began to formalise engagements through a written deed, in order to better protect the rights of women in the partnership. The deeds mostly consist of prenuptial conditions to be imposed on the husband: where the couple would live (and who has the right to choose), the right of the woman to ask for a divorce, various restrictions on the husband’s movemen

The work is a collection of halakhic rulings (called מעשה in the sense of 'legal ruling'). The abbreviation מע׳ (for מעשה) is used before each section. This fragment was first edited by B.M. Levin, 'Geniza Fragments' (משרידי הגניזה), Tarbiz 2 (1931), 410-515; but see also the edition in the monograph by Hillel Newman, המעשים לבני ארץ־ישראל : הלכה והיסטוריה בארץ־ישראל הביזנטית ('Maʻasim of the people of the land of Israel : Halakha and history in Byzantine Palestine', 2011), esp. 22, 176-93. As well as preserving a very sparsely attested text, the fragment is noteworthy for the poor quality piece of parchment from which the bifolium is made.

MS-LL-00001-00010.c: Manuscripts, English (Old); Illumination of books and manuscripts, Anglo-Saxon; Prayer books ; The Book of Cerne is a prayerbook made in Mercia, probably in the 820s. It is one of the most interesting and least famous of early Anglo-Saxon illuminated manuscripts, over-shadowed by the compelling presence of the great Insular gospel books, bibles and psalters and by the prodigious works of Bede and Aldhelm. Yet this complex and visually attractive book, and its relationships with other artefacts of its period, cast a strong beam of light upon the history and culture of its age and upon the kingdom of Mercia. The sobriquet 'The Book of Cerne' stems from the book's later medieval provenance, for the 9th-century manuscript is now sandwiched between two lengthy sequences of documentary and liturgical materials from the monastery of Cerne Abbas in Dorset. These date from the 14th to the 16th century and are unlikely to have been added to the manuscript during the Middle Ages, and possibly not until after 1697 (when the manuscript was recorded in the possession of John Moore, with only the copy of the Magna Carta noted in addition to the 9th-century contents). MS-LL-00001-00018.c: Medicine; Cooking, Medieval; Heraldry; Hunting ; Down to about the end of the 14th century most manuscript books were typically made either by professional scribes working for hire, or by some who would practise the craft by vocation, in religious houses or other ecclesiastical environments. Thereafter, it became increasingly common for a variety of lay persons (lawyers, merchants, estate managers, the numerous unbeneficed clergy, and the like) to construct and copy manuscripts for their own use, or for that of a small circle of associates, such as a household or a family. The spread of pragmatic literacy among professionals, for such purposes as accounting and correspondence, rapidly increased the circulation of paper as the preferred material for writing, and the making of books as a means of keeping texts useful for many practical purposes, or for edification or entertainment, became common practice. The physical construction of such manuscripts was often accretive, the compiler accumulating a series of paper gatherings and booklets as exemplars became available. MS-LL-00002-00002.c: Theology; Sermons, medieval ; The sermons of Jacobus de Voragine (d. 1298) form the principal contents of this manuscript. The Sermones de tempore per annum siue sermones dominicales (ff. 15r-127r ) were, as their name suggests, for preaching on Sundays; the Sermones de sanctis (ff. 137r-256v ) for preaching on saints' feast days. This practical arrangement complemented the Church's liturgical calendar, and is reflected in other books used or read as part of this: for instance, the differentiation in the biblical readings provided in breviaries between the 'Temporale' and the 'Sanctorale'. Except for the first and sixth quires of the Sermones de tempore (Quires 2 and 7 - see Collation), these sermon compilations were copied by a single scribe: a William of 'Eglisfehan' - presumably Ecclefechan - who recorded his name and motto on f. 127r , and repeated the latter on f. 256v . This William, or more likely another contemporary scribe, supplemented these with a collection of twenty-six anonymous 'Sermones de mortuis' - for preaching at funerals - which he copied onto a separate quire bound in between these two (ff. 129r-136r ). MS-LL-00002-00013.c: Bible. Gospels ; This Greek Gospel book was produced at the end of 15th century for the humanist scholar Guillaume Budé (b. 1468, d. 1540) by Georgios Hermonymos of Sparta (b. c. 1430, d. c. 1511), who in addition to being a copyist, was also a diplomat (he was sent to England by Pope Sixtus IV) and the first lecturer of Greek at the Collège de Sorbonne in Paris. The manuscript was meant to be a grand copy, made with high quality parchment, initials decorated or traced with gold ink, as well as marginal summaries, running heads and a final colophon. The original cover is lost and replaced by a medium quality one. Hermonymos also copied CUL Kk.5.35, Kk.6.23, Nn.4.2 and Corpus Christi College, Parker Library, Cambridge, MS 224; Kk.5.35 and Ll.2.13 have in common the Gospels and two final texts from Psellus and Gregory of Nazianus. It is possible that one of the two manuscripts is a copy of the other. Dr Matteo Di Franco

MS-LL-00005-00004.c: This manuscript contains a Compilation of notes and transcriptions of Greek texts , copied by the 17th-century clergyman and writer Abednego Seller, around 1686. Most of the content was copied from identified manuscripts at Lincoln College, Oxford, where Seller studied, and at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge. The principal text is a commentary on Aristotle's Metaphysics which is the primary surviving work of the 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher Syrianus. The rest of the manuscript's content consists of excerpts, from texts including other commentaries on the works of Plato and Aristotle, a commentary on the Odyssey , mathematical and astronomical works and Procopius of Caesarea's history of the building works of the Emperor Justinian I. The excerpts from the Topographia Christiana of Cosmas Indicopleustes, which include a number of descriptions of animals, have been illustrated with two ink drawings of animals on p. 6 bis . One other work appears in full, a short medical text from the Hippocratic corpus. MS-LL-00005-00018.d: Fifteenth century. This is ratified by the dateable texts contained in MS Ll.5.18, which accommodate production from quite early in the first half of the century. The Life of Saint Margaret , commissioned by Edmund Mortimer, was composed by John Lydgate between 1415-26 and the version of the Life of Saint Dorothy contained in MS Ll.5.18 has been identified by Manfred Görlach to be one of a group of the tale that dates from the early fifteenth century.

MS-LL-00005-00018.c: Devotional literature, English (Middle) ; Cambridge University Library MS Ll.5.18 is a small fifteenth-century miscellany, consisting of a selection of devotional vernacular texts: the final portion of the treatise The Direccion of a Mannys Lyfe , The Life and The Charter of the Abbey of the Holy Ghost , the Life of Saint Dorothy , a translated excerpt from Saint Augustine’s De contemptu mundi and John Lydgate’s Life of Saint Margaret . As such, it can offer us a valuable insight into personal spiritual practices in the late medieval period. Currently, the provenance of the manuscript remains a matter of supposition. That said, it can be firmly situated among a well-documented manuscript tradition from the period in which miscellanies present female saints’ vitae and/or Marian material along with the Abbey and Charter . British Library MS Harley 5272, for example, bears close textual parallels to MS Ll.5.18, containing both the Abbey and Charter in addition to a verse life of Saint Dorothy and Lydgate’s Life of Our Lady . MS-MAGDALENE-COLLEGE-PEPYS-00878.c: Medicine, Medieval ; This manuscript contains a large number of medical treatises, and medical recipes alongside instructions of a magical, cosmetic, practical, equestrian, and horticultural nature. The collection also includes a previously unidentified selection of recipes from the Treatises of fistula in ano: haemorrhoids, and clysters by the London surgeon John Arderne (1307–1392) on pp. 156-160 . An adaptation made to one of Arderne's recipes on p. 160 , called a 'Valence of Wormwood', may give an insight into the scribe's background. Arderne's original version reports how the surgeon used this medicine to heal a fisherman from London who had injured his arm on a sharp iron attached to the door of the monastery of the Carmelites or White Friars [see D'Arcy Power (1910), pp. 100, 133-134]. However, the version in Pepys MS 878 has been updated with what appears to be another medical practitioner's testimony: "This medicine I have often used and praised because with it I healed a sheriff at Bristol who endured a puncture wound in the muscle of his left arm from a small dagger while separating two (fighting) men and he was close to death because of the pain, swelling, burning, and

MS-MAGDALENE-COLLEGE-PEPYS-00911.t: A 'Sortes' manuscript including the Experimentarius attributed to Bernardus Silvestris
MS-MAGDALENE-COLLEGE-PEPYS-00911.c: Astrology, Early Works to 1800; Astrology ; Cambridge, Magdalene College, MS Pepys 911 (hereafter Pepys 911) is a beautifully illustrated example of a type of medieval book known as a ' sortes ' manuscript, essentially a genre of medieval book concerned with various aspects of what we now describe as divination, prognostication, and fortune-telling. Sortes manuscripts seem to have been quite a popular genre of medieval book, and among those that were made in medieval north-western Europe the majority of the surviving sortes manuscripts contain various combinations of a core group of texts attributed (spuriously) to illustrious Classical figures such as Pythagoras and Cicero. The various sortes texts popular in medieval north-western Europe follow a similar pattern for use. They typically begin with a list of questions, for example: Should the reader get married? Will a pregnant woman give birth to a boy or a girl? Or will a missing item be found? The reader is then guided into choosing a random number (typically between 1-10) by throwing dice or turning a wheel or another specified method. MS-MAGDALENE-COLLEGE-PEPYS-01047.c: Medicine, Medieval ; This manuscript contains a large collection of medical and culinary recipes in Middle English. It also contains a compilation of selections from the instruction manual in Middle English prose and verse that was known as the The Book of Hawking, Hunting, and Blasing of Arms or The Boke of St Albans . This work was first printed by the so-called Schoolmaster Printer at St Albans in 1486. This print includes a treatise on hunting ( The manere of huntynge for all manere of bestys ) that partly takes the form of an instruction from a 'Dame' to her 'child' and associates it with a 'Dam Julyans Barnes' in its colophon: "Explicit Dam Julyans Barnes in her boke of huntyng.". Pepys MS 1047 does not contain materials from this hunting treatise but a selection from additional materials that follow it in the 1486 print of The Boke of St Albans . Although these additional materials are not associated with 'Dam Julyans Barnes', Pepys MS 1047 does refer to her at the end of one of its texts (see f. 5v : 'Explicit Julyan Barne'). MS-MAGDALENE-COLLEGE-PEPYS-01307.c: Medicine, Medieval ; This compact manuscript once owned by Samuel Pepys, is, for the most part, a redaction of the popular medical text known as the Antidotarium Nicholai . The manuscript also contains a shorter and extensively reorganised version of the information in the Antidotarium Nicholai and a treatise on uroscopy that is part of the 'Dome of Uryne' group of texts identified by M. T. Tavormina. Little is known about the history of the manuscript prior to it coming into the possession of Samuel Pepys, but the palaeography and orthography of the volume suggest that it was made in England, probably in Norfolk, in the second quarter of the 15th century. The majority of this manuscript is given over to two redactions of the Antidotarium Nicholai , both in Middle English, although the first retains many of the chapter headings from the Latin versions of the text. The larger of the two (ff. 1r-40v ) presents the text in a more typical form, with the medicinal preparations described in alphabetical order and each supplied with instructions for making the medicinal preparation followed by dosage instructions. MS-MANC-RYL-PERS-00008.c: Oriental black morocco binding with sunk medallions and pendants, much worn, and with European early 19th-century light brown gilt calf back inscribed SHAN (sic) NAMEH. doublures of Indian kincob. Back cover detached.Folio 1r contains inscriptions and seals. The binding needs repair, otherwise the rest of the manuscript is in a very good condition, apart from deliberate damage to the miniatures. There is a double title- page illumination on ff. 1v-2r, and further illuminated unvans on ff. 15v (the start of the poem) and 270v (the start of the reign of Luhrasp). The first two pages are slightly torn. There is no colophon on this ms. However, there is an added folio (f 581) which seems to be a reconstruction of the last folio. This too does not contain any information about the attribution of the work, which Robinson identifies as an excellent example of the Shiraz style of the mid 16th century. There are altogether 19 miniatures, sometimes savagely defaced; the choice of scene in the first part of the ms. is unusual, omitting many popular subjects. Robinson identifies the work of two different artists. (A.M.).BibliographyB.W. Robinson, Persian paintings in the John Rylands Library,

The information recorded here refers only to the Shahnama.The ms. begins with the 'old' preface to the Shahnama, f. 1v; the poem starts on f. 7v and the second book, with the reign of Luhrasp, on f. 359v. Each of these pages contains an illuminated heading. These are in the un-outlined style associated with Muzaffarid Shiraz of second half of the 15th century. The colophons contain no details - the final page is a modern replacement. The text includes the Barzunama, following the story of Bizhan and Manizha.The ms. contains 42 miniatures, 2 preliminary sketches and 11 blank spaces, indicating an original intention to include 55 paintings. The pictures are all very rubbed and damaged.Robinson identifies two artists at work, Painter A was probably an Indian, his primitive and naïve style recalling Jalayirid work, as especially evident from his palette (oranges and mauves). MS-MANC-RYL-PERS-00869.c: Some images from this manuscript are available for viewing on the John Rylands University Library website, where the volume is dated 1812 (= 1227 AH). The manuscript was included in the exhibition in the Library in 2010. The text is in four sections, each marked by a large 'unvan, and clearly not completed in chronological order: Section one ends on f. 169r, with a colophon dated 1237 AH. Folios 169v and 170r are blank. Section two starts on f. 170v with the story of Bizhan and Manizha, and ends on f. 282r, with a colophon dated 11 Ramadan 1235 (22 June 1820). Folios 282v and 283r are blank. Section three starts on f. 283v and ends on f. 417v, with a colophon dated "the time of Friday prayer at the beginning of Muharram 1235" (beg. 20 October 1819). Section four starts facing f. 418r (?), with the reign of Aushirvan, although the rubrics repeat the rubrics from the story of Bizhan and Manizha, followed by the Davazdah Rukh, i.e. due to scribal error. Inspected by ChM, 19 March 2004 and 8 December 2007, report not yet finalised.

MS-MM-00001-00011.c: Greek drama (Tragedy) ; This mid-14th century working text manuscript transmits the so-called 'Byzantine triad' of three plays of Euripides (b. c. 480, d. 406 BC), selected for study in Byzantine schools: Hecuba , Orestes and Phoenician Women . The first section ( ff. 1r-33v ) comprises Hecuba and Orestes ll. 1-133, and the text follows the recension (i.e. redaction) of the Byzantine grammarian Manuel Moschopoulus (13th-14th century; see Turyn (1957), p. 123-124). The second section ( ff. 34r-107v ) contains Orestes ll. 134-end and Phoenician Women , in the recension of Byzantine grammarian Thomas Magistros (13th-14th century), and is accompanied by scholia of the same scholar. The order of quires from ff. 41r to 68v is inverted, and an English hand has noted the order of lines. Richard Porson, Regius Professor of Greek at Cambridge (b. 1759, d. 1808), used this manuscript (siglum Cant) in his edition of Euripides' tragedies (see the second edition, 1802 ). J. Diggle designated the manuscript with siglum Mm in his edition of Phoenician Women (Oxford, 1994); the manuscript is also designated as Zx for scholia by Günther (1995). MS-MM-00001-00017.e: Codex 1 + 132 Leaf height: ca. 220/225 mm, width: 160-164 mm.
MS-MM-00001-00017.c: Medicine, Greek and Roman ; This manuscript contains a miscellany of Greek medical texts , comprising writings by Oribasius and pseudo-Alexander of Aphrodisias, as well as an anonymous collection of recipes. The codex is formed of three parts, all written by the same scribe, Michael Souliardos, at the beginning of the 16th century, as indicated by the watermarks. Born in Nauplion, Souliardos was active in Greece and in Italy, where this manuscript was probably copied. Another manuscript copied by him is preserved at Cambridge University Library, MS Dd.11.70 . MS Mm.1.17 was owned by the Parisian physician Jacques Mentel (1597-1671) and later acquired by Jean-Baptiste Hautin (probably a relative of the French scholar and numismatist Jean-Baptiste Hautin, ca. 1580-1640). When Hautin had the manuscript, its parts were certainly already bound together, as is indicated by the fact that, in a handwritten note on the left pastedown, he recorded the inclusion among the manuscript's contents of " Oribasii tractatus varii", and a work by Oribasius is present in part II. MS-MM-00005-00002-MSI.d: 1450-75, based on the circulation of the paper stocks
MS-MM-00005-00002-MSI.c: The materials in Mm.5.2 combine readings, notes, mnemonic texts, and Year Books. It includes the New Tenures of Sir Thomas Littleton (d. 1482); miscellaneous mnemonics and other notes; a reading on chapters 32 to 39 of Westminster II; the Year Book for 2 Henry VI; a mnemonic note on the ‘five ages of woman’, and the Year Book for 9 Henry V (CELM, pp. 490-2). A paper manuscript of 115 folios. Each folio measures about 306 mm in height x 215 mm in width, and the sheets are folded in folio. This suggests that the original sheets had dimensions ranging between 310 mm in height x 440 mm in width, a format of paper known as Chancery, which was the most common size of paper in medieval England. The range of measurements depends on the precise dimensions of the original sheets before folding and the trimming (or not) of the folio before binding. There are four paper stocks in this manuscript, including marks of a cart (f. 31 appears on Bernstein as Briquet 3548 , dated to Catania, 1475; the watermark in this example of the stock has moved a bit, but such movement is reasonable over the use of the mould); a coat of arms surmounted by a crown, and a hand surmounted by a six-petal flower.
